Volume One. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu,
Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Recipient of the Purple Robe.
I take refuge in the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, And in the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, Who dwell throughout all the infinite worlds In the ten directions.

The wise should know that a human body is difficult to obtain, and it is likewise difficult to accomplish all sublime practices within a single moment; if one does not give rise to contemplation and perform deeds of benefit during this time, this life has come in vain.
How can one develop a diligent and courageous mind to receive and listen to the Tathāgata’s pure teachings?
There are two matters: namely, that a human body is difficult to obtain, the True Dharma is difficult to hear, and to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world is even more difficult.
Question:
By what means is it proven that encountering a Buddha is extremely difficult?
Answer:
This is stated in countless sūtras and serves as the definitive authority.
Furthermore, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "O Bhikṣus!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in this world only once in a vast expanse of time spanning hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas; such an appearance by a Tathāgata is exceedingly rare, occurring only as rarely as the udumbara flower appearing once in an age.
The *Niyatārāja-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Ānanda!
When the Buddhas appear in the world, the udumbara flower appears simultaneously."
The flowers are like gold, possessing pure and wondrous radiance.
When they bloom, their extraordinary fragrance pervades within a yojana.

The light of these flowers can dispel darkness; it enables those who contemplate them to attain immediate purity; it can alleviate the suffering of illness, provide brilliant illumination, eliminate foul odors, and bestow sublime fragrances. That fragrance can pacify the increase or decrease of the four elements.

Furthermore, these flowers do not appear everywhere even for a universal wheel-turning king; they manifest only for a golden wheel-turning king. How much less so for sentient beings who violate the precepts? Only when a Buddha appears in the world do these flowers emerge together with him.
In this regard, how can one know whether that *udumbara* flower exists or not during vast intervals of time?

As it is said in the *Nidāna-saṃyukta*: "To the north of the great lake Anavatapta there is a mountain named Pañcaśikhara; upon that mountain is a grove of *udumbara* flowers. When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, descends from the Tuṣita heaven to be born among humans and enters his mother’s womb, those *udumbara* flowers first form buds.
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emerges from his mother’s womb, these flowers grow and manifest the appearance of full bloom."
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, attained the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, those *udumbara* flowers bloomed in profusion;
when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, relinquished his life-span and conditioned activities, these flowers withered and decayed;
and when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, entered *nirvāṇa*, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of these trees all fell away.
The size of those flowers was as large as a chariot wheel.
The *Vipula-jñāna-vaipulya-sūtra* states that the Greatly Renowned King of Sages addressed the assembly of sages, saying:
"O virtuous ones!"
If a bodhisattva, even for a brief moment, encounters a Tathāgata appearing in the world to preach the Dharma and bring benefit through transformation, this constitutes true correspondence.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "To encounter a Buddha’s appearance in the world throughout millions of kalpas, and to hear, receive, respect, and faithfully believe the True Dharma—this true vision is exceedingly difficult to obtain."

The *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* states that after this Bhadrakalpa, for sixty-five kalpas no Buddha shall appear in the world. Thereafter, there will be a kalpa named Mahāyaśas, in which ten thousand Buddhas will appear in the world.

After the eon of Great Renown, for eighty thousand eons no Buddha appeared in the world. Subsequently, there was an eon named Star-like (Tārakopama), in which eighty thousand Buddhas appeared in the world.

After the eon likened to a star, three hundred eons passed without a Buddha appearing in the world. Subsequently, there was an eon named *Guṇavyūha* (Adorned with Virtues), during which eighty-four thousand Buddhas appeared in the world.
In this regard, the question is asked:
"How can one know that a human body is difficult to obtain?
The answer is:
In all the various sūtras, it is stated as follows.
As the *Saṃyukta Āgama* says, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!"

It is like the great earth filled with flowing water; suppose someone takes a piece of wood, makes a hole in it, and places it in the water. This wood floats lightly and drifts along with the wind: if there is an east wind, it moves westward; if there is a west wind, it moves eastward; and it is the same when blown by winds from the south or north.

There is a one-eyed turtle living within that water, with a lifespan of countless hundreds of years; once every hundred years, it surfaces from the water and attempts to thrust its head through the hole in the log. O Bhikṣus!
What do you think?
If that one-eyed turtle has such an extremely long life and surfaces only once every hundred years, would it be possible for it to encounter the hole in the floating log?
The bhikṣus said:
"No, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said: "O Bhikṣus!
To encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world, to receive his teaching and transformation, to awaken to the Right Path, and to attain Nirvāṇa is likewise so extremely difficult."
Furthermore, it is difficult to obtain a human body endowed with the fullness of its constituent parts.
Here, a question is asked:
How is it known that being endowed with the fullness of parts is difficult to obtain?
Answer: It is stated thus in various sūtras.
As it says in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha said:
"O Bhikṣus! There are eight kinds of obstacles; when people do not recognize these times, they should not practice the holy life (brahmacarya). What are the eight? "

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and liberating sentient beings so that they reach nirvana, yet there is a class of sentient beings within the hells—this is the first difficulty regarding the timing for practicing the holy life.

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and delivering sentient beings so that they reach nirvana, yet a certain class of sentient beings remains among the animals—this is the second difficulty regarding the timing for practicing the holy life.

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and delivering sentient beings so that they reach nirvana, yet a certain class of sentient beings remains among the hungry ghosts—this is the third difficulty regarding the timing for practicing the holy life.

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and liberating sentient beings so that they reach nirvana, yet a certain class of sentient beings remains in the Heaven of Long Life (Ābhāsvara), this constitutes the fourth difficulty regarding the timing for practicing the holy life.

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and delivering sentient beings so that they reach nirvāṇa, yet there are certain classes of sentient beings dwelling in remote, evil, and violent regions—this is the fifth difficulty regarding the timing for practicing the holy life.

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and delivering sentient beings so that they reach nirvana, yet there are certain classes of sentient beings who, though born in a central land, are either deaf or mute and lack complete faculties, such that they do not understand the meaning of what is well-spoken or ill-spoken—this is the sixth difficulty regarding the timing for one practicing the holy life.

If a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential teachings of the Dharma, transforming and delivering sentient beings so that they reach Nirvana, yet there is a class of sentient beings born in a central land who are neither deaf nor mute and possess all six sense faculties intact, being fully capable of discerning both well-spoken and ill-spoken words, but who nevertheless give rise to false views and inverted attachments—claiming there is no giving and no benefit, no fire-sacrifices, no karmic fruits and retributions of good or evil deeds, no this world and no other world, no father and no mother, no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world, no right path or right practice, and no arhats who, through their own supernormal powers, realize the holy fruit in this world and the next—this is the seventh difficulty regarding the timing for practicing the holy life.

Furthermore, there may be a class of sentient beings born in a central land, who are neither deaf nor mute and possess all six sense faculties intact; they are capable of discerning both well-spoken and ill-spoken words, and they possess right view free from inverted attachments, such as believing that there is giving, there is merit, and even that there are Arhats who have realized the fruits of sainthood. Yet, because a Buddha has not appeared in the world and does not teach the essential Dharma, this constitutes the eighth difficulty regarding the timing for one who practices the holy life.

"O Bhikṣus! You should know that there is one particular conjunction of circumstances at which time one ought to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). That is: when a Buddha appears in the world and proclaims the essential points of the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; profound in both letter and meaning; pure and unadulterated; and fully endowed with the characteristics of the clear and white holy life."

Furthermore, there are certain sentient beings born in a central land who are neither deaf nor mute, possessing all six sense faculties intact; they are able to fully comprehend both well-spoken and ill-spoken words, are endowed with right view and do not give rise to inverted attachments, such as believing that there is giving, there is sacrifice, and there is the offering of fire; that there are wholesome and unwholesome deeds and their respective karmic fruits and retributions; that there is this world and another world; that there are fathers and mothers; that there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world; that there is the right path and the right way; and that there are arhats who, through their own supernormal powers, have realized the noble fruit in this world and the next. This is called the first convergence of conditions.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, "Candraprabha-parivarta," states: "O noble ones!
The convergence of seasonal factors, like a fragrant tree that blossoms according to its proper time, is exceedingly rare."
In this regard, one should ask:
For those who have attained a human body, how can they obtain the pure and equanimous purity of what is taught?
Answer:
If ten kinds of merit can be perfected, one will attain the purity and equality of a human body. What are these ten?
As stated in the *Atikrānta-nīcakulāsūtra*: first, if a son or daughter of good family has internally generated the bodhicitta, they immediately give rise to pure faith;
Second, having vast and pure desire to see the noble ones;
third, delighting in hearing the true Dharma;
fourth, not giving rise to stinginess or envy, but universally practicing great generosity.
Fifth, maintaining an upright body and fixing the mind on the path to Nirvana;
sixth, practicing extensive giving with an unimpeded and virtuous mind;
seventh, believing in the existence of all karmas and their respective retributions.
Eighth, not giving rise to conceptual discrimination;
ninth, being without seeking, without doubt, and possessing undefiled wisdom;
tenth, not undermining the karmic fruits of good and evil deeds.
Once these ten kinds [of factors] have been understood, one should refrain from all unwholesome actions regarding the conditions for this life.
Herein, it should be asked:
what is meant by "faith"?
Answer: Faith means turning toward the noble ones and refraining from all evil deeds.
As it is said in the *Dharmasamudgata-sūtra*:
Among all wholesome dharmas, faith is the precursor.
What is the meaning of this "faith"?
It means the sense of compliance and accord.

This one is fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s unobstructed wisdom and is able to proclaim the profound, true Dharma that is difficult to see and difficult to know, forever severing the fetters of craving.

That is to say: there is no eye and no cessation of the eye; no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, and no cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no abiding and no non-abiding; no intention and no non-intention. Possessing sixty kinds of melodic tones and phrases, their sequential vocal karma is pure and immaculate; their bodies are utterly purified, and their minds manifest various forms and signs.
The Buddha-Tathāgata knows all and sees all; there is nothing he does not realize or comprehend.

With the pure eye and the universal eye of a Tathāgata—having forever severed faults and distanced himself from craving, having shattered the darkness of ignorance and surpassed the physical eye—he is able to contemplate the profound cranial mark (*uṣṇīṣa*) and proclaim the unsurpassed, supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Although all Buddha-dharmas are conceptually differentiated, to not misrepresent such Buddha-dharmas as being contrary to dependent origination is called faith.
The *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* states that the Buddha said: "O Mañjuśrī!"
What is called the power of faith?

It refers to the direct confirmation and conformity with all Buddha-dharmas; it is the conviction and understanding free from doubt and free from seeking anything else, being a resolute and true faith in karma and its retribution.

With faith free from confusion, one generates pure confidence in all practices performed through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as in all phenomena; that is to say: there is the fruit of giving for giving, the fruit of ethical discipline for ethical discipline, the fruit of patience for patience, the fruit of diligence for diligence, the fruit of meditative concentration for meditative concentration, and the fruit of wisdom for wisdom.
When one speaks thus of these characteristics of purity,
being able to generate pure faith within the superior resolve for the Mahāyāna is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
Furthermore, if one further awakens to and understands all attachments, this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Whether as faculties (*indriya*) or powers (*bala*), they are collectively termed faith (*śraddhā*).
Furthermore, in this context, what is called the power of faith?
Faith means sealing and conforming; it is that which is able to believe in the voices of others.
What is it for a practitioner of the bodhisattva path to rely on the voices of others?

It refers to hearing the instructions of others and thereby generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva; that is, the bodhisattva relies upon the sounds of the *pāramitās*, skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), all the Buddha-dharmas, and the bodhisattva-dharmas.
Having heard it from another, one gives rise to supreme pure faith; this is called the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).
The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"Śāriputra!..."

This practitioner of the bodhisattva path, having internally generated the bodhicitta, immediately gives rise to pure faith and vast purification. Desiring to see the noble ones and delighting in hearing the true Dharma, they possess resolute conviction in the existence of all karmas and their karmic fruits and retributions. They abandon the ten unwholesome actions and cultivate the ten wholesome actions; they believe in the existence of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have correctly entered the right path and are themselves well-learned. What they hear accords with their minds, bringing harmony to their thoughts; they transcend doubt and do not undergo further existence. Constantly drawing near to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas—their true spiritual friends—they give rise to affection and respect, and they believe in the various karmas and their karmic fruits and retributions as taught by those spiritual friends.

Having understood their capacities, he should deliver for them the appropriate profound discourses: namely, the discourse on emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, and non-origination; the discourse on the absence of self, person, sentient being, and life-sustainer; and the discourse on dependent origination.

Having heard these various discourses, one is without doubt and likewise without attachment; one enters into all phenomena, remaining entirely unattached to the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so forth.
One has faith that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and through the pursuit of Buddha-wisdom, remains single-mindedly and without negligence.
What is called "heedfulness" (*apramāda*)?
It means that when the sense faculties give rise to distraction, one should discipline one's own mind and protect the minds of others.

The *Candraprabhabodhisattva-sūtra* states: "If sentient beings develop pure faith toward the Three Jewels, this is truly difficult to attain; it is, for example, as difficult to obtain as a wish-fulfilling jewel."
The *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* states that the noble Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"There are five kinds of dharmas through which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to resolute conviction; by doing so, they will fully attain all those various incalculable and most supreme merits."

What are these five? First, all phenomena are empty; second, all phenomena have no antidote; third, all phenomena are unarisen; fourth, all phenomena are unceasing; fifth, all phenomena are ineffable.

One should develop resolute conviction regarding these five kinds [of activities]: although the Tathāgata has no conscious arousal of thought nor any conceptual discrimination regarding the various modes of deportment and spheres of activity throughout the lands of Jambudvīpa, numbering more than the atoms of dust, he nevertheless constantly manifests them at all times—whether opportune or inopportune—in accordance with the mental dispositions of sentient beings.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to resolute conviction regarding this.

As stated in the *Saṃghasūtra-nidāna-sūtra*, for the sake of transforming and benefiting sentient beings, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, cultivated all practices throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to faith and understanding in this.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, received his prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha; thereafter, he cultivated supreme practices throughout that interval, universally entering the realms of all Buddhas for boundless eons, until finally manifesting perfect enlightenment even unto today.
One should give rise to faith and understanding regarding this.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, having witnessed the circumstances of the slaughter of the Śākya clan, for the sake of transforming and delivering sentient beings and bringing them benefit, cultivated supreme practices throughout boundless kalpas and manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
One should give rise to faith and understanding regarding this.
Therefore, it should be known that for all sentient beings, if they should resolve upon bodhicitta, this is difficult to attain.
Question:
It is truly difficult to give rise to the bodhicitta. How, then, is it to be generated? Answer:
There are many sūtras that speak of this.
For instance, according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is truly difficult for sentient beings in the world to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One should know that the bodhicitta is like a seed of the world, for it plants all the wholesome dharmas of the world;
it is like the realm of all Buddha-dharmas, for it can utterly incinerate all evil deeds.
It is like the fire at the end of an eon (*kalpāgni*), for it can dissolve and destroy all unwholesome dharmas.
It is like the great earth, for it can bring all meanings to fulfillment.
It is like the king of *maṇi* jewels, for it completely fulfills all aspirations.
It is like a precious vase, for it extracts one from the stream of birth and death.
It is like a supreme hook and bait, for all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—as well as all Buddha-dharmas and all Buddha-qualities, universally extol the merit of that bodhicitta.
It is like a stupa or temple of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because it contains within it the supreme spheres of all bodhisattva practices.
Furthermore, this bodhicitta gives birth to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Son of good family!

It is like a medicine called Iron-Gold Light; a single *liang* of this medicine can transform a thousand *liang* of iron, causing it all to become gold. Those thousand *liang* of iron cannot destroy this single *liang* of sacred medicine.

It is the same for one who has resolved upon bodhicitta: if they can once generate the mind of omniscience, which is embraced by the wisdom of dedicating roots of goodness through the subtle and sublime medicinal elixir, it can cause all karmic and afflictive obstructions to be transformed entirely into the gold of all dharmas and omniscience; those karmic and afflictive obstructions cannot defile the mind of omniscience.

Good son! It is like holding a single torch and entering a dark room; as soon as one enters the room, the gloom accumulated over hundreds or thousands of years is entirely destroyed, and it becomes brilliantly illuminated.

The arousal of the bodhicitta is likewise so: grasping the great radiant torch of the mind of omniscience, one enters the dark chamber of the mental continuum of sentient beings. As one enters therein, all the darkness of ignorance—the obscurations of karma and afflictions accumulated over unspeakable hundreds of thousands of kalpas—is entirely eliminated, and the brilliant illumination of the light of great wisdom is brought forth.
"Good son! Furthermore, it is like a great dragon king who wears upon his head a crown made of the supreme, wondrous wish-fulfilling jewel; no enemy dares to come and threaten him with fear.

So too it is with all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: wearing upon their heads the crown of the supreme, wondrous wish-fulfilling jewels of the bodhicitta and great compassion, no evils of any miserable realms dare to come and threaten them with fear."

Furthermore, even if one were to gather together all the gold, silver, precious jewels, flower garlands, garments, and exquisite articles of pleasure that are manifested within the most brilliantly illuminated sphere of the pure, perfect orb of the sun and moon, the total value of all these things combined could not equal the price of a single King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels (cintāmaṇi-rāja).

The generation of the bodhicitta is likewise so: to the extent that it illuminates the dharma-realm of the path of omniscience throughout the three periods of time, within that sphere appear all sentient beings, all devas and humans, as well as all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; yet all their roots of goodness, whether with outflows or without outflows, cannot equal the value of the sovereign jewel-king that is the generation of the bodhicitta.

Furthermore, it is like the milk of cattle and sheep filling the great ocean; when even a single drop from the footprint of a lioness’s milk falls into the sea, the various milks of cattle and sheep cannot coagulate nor can they harmonize with it.

The bodhicitta is also like this: though the various karmas and afflictions accumulated over hundreds of thousands of unspeakable eons may be like a great ocean, when a single drop of milk—the mind of omniscience—emitted by the Tathāgata, the Great Man, the Lion, falls into that sea, all karmas and afflictions are forever exhausted without remainder, and even all the liberations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot coexist with it.
Furthermore, just as one who associates with a person of valor cannot be harmed by any enemies or malevolent forces, so too it is for one who has resolved upon bodhicitta:
if they associate with a courageous bodhisattva, no enemies of unwholesome actions can cause them harm.

Furthermore, it is like a precious diamond that, though damaged and incomplete, remains the most excellent among all jewels; it surpasses all other ornaments, its name as "diamond jewel" is never lost, and it is universally able to relieve the poverty of all beings.

A small portion of the bodhicitta is likewise so: it is like a fragmentary diamond gem; though not yet fully complete, it still surpasses the adornments of all the merits of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, its name as a bodhisattva is never extinguished, and it is able to rescue those who are impoverished and lack the wealth of the noble ones.
The *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchāsūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Great King!
Excellent, excellent!"
You are able to love, delight in, and aspire to the Buddha-dharma. O Great King!

Just as you currently govern and transform the Kingdom of Kośala, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all the people, rescuing and delivering them, comforting and guiding them so that they return to the Right Path.

However, if you are able to extensively benefit all sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the mind of omniscience, to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, and to advance toward the realization of the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that would be an even greater benefit.
Furthermore, Great King!
In that Jeta Grove, there are always hundreds of thousands of sages and holy ones dwelling in seclusion; you should conceive a sense of respect toward it, Great King!

Those noble and holy ones have a longing for the Perfectly Awakened One; they possess faith, a quest, an aspiration, and praise, giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy. These noble and holy ones generate the utmost faith and reverence through their body, speech, and mind.
Why is this? Great King!

Because in that region there have appeared hundreds of countless Buddhas, hundreds of countless turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, and hundreds of countless assemblies of noble ones who have attained liberation in succession.

In this manner, even until countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Ganges-sands of Buddhas appear in the world, turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma and transforming the assembly of noble ones—likewise, all those sages and worthies give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, as well as faith, seeking, and vows.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Dharma-protector (Dharmarakṣa), a Śramaṇa of Purple Robes and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma (Chuánfàn Dàshī), concurrently serving as Vice-Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù Shǎoqīng), and others: The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"For example, when a lion is first born, it possesses power and majesty from the very moment of its birth. Should there be any herd of deer in its path, upon merely smelling the scent of the lion, they all flee in terror."

Suppose even a powerful dragon-elephant, upon smelling the scent of a lion, becomes distressed and terrified, wrenching at its chains and bonds; once those bonds are severed, it bolts in all four directions, searching everywhere among mountain crags and earth caves for a place to hide.
Even aquatic creatures and winged birds are terrified upon smelling the scent of a lion. Mañjuśrī,
it is just the same for bodhisattvas who possess the power of wisdom.

As soon as that Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment gives rise to the great mind of Bodhicitta, he immediately surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the palaces of Māra tremble, and all the celestial Māras are struck with terror. Because of this terror, they are all unable to remain at ease within their palaces.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: The Buddha said,
"Ānanda, what do you think?"
"It is as if there were a person whose hands and feet were both severed; would they still be able to remain alive?
Ānanda replied, "Even though their hands and feet are severed, their life would still continue."
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Suppose there were someone who had their heart torn open; would that person be able to remain alive?"
Ānanda replied: "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! You should know that my disciples Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra are like my hands and feet, whereas the bodhisattvas are like my own heart."

Ānanda! If there is a bodhisattva who drives a great precious chariot, performing supernatural feats through the merits of the five desires, yet has no one to drive it for him, the Tathāgata at that time shall personally drive the chariot for that bodhisattva to advance upon the path.
If Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were to cultivate the three gates of liberation for an eon or even beyond an eon, the Tathāgata would no longer need to exert effort to urge them forward.
The *Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra* states: "O Bhikṣus!

Even if all the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to praise for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges the treasury of merits belonging to one who has generated the mind associated with omniscience, they could not exhaustively describe them."

Why is this? Because when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, there was never even for a moment that he did not give rise to this mind, embracing all sentient beings without exception.
Having thus gathered them in, he likewise does not give rise to the notion that sentient beings are those to be converted.

Throughout the entire infinite realm of sentient beings, the Tathāgata has pervaded that realm, cultivating the vast and supreme practices of a bodhisattva, and with each and every resolve, he has accumulated a multitude of merit-accumulations.
Why is this so? O Bhikṣus!
The realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible.

Because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the Tathāgata extensively cultivates the sublime practices of a bodhisattva; likewise, each and every arousal of the mind that accumulates the aggregates of merit is also inexhaustible.

The *Tathāgataguhyasūtra* states: "If bodhisattvas resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate sublime practices, they shall ensure that the lineage of the Three Jewels remains uninterrupted and unceasing."

Furthermore, it is said that the mass of merit born from a bodhisattva’s bodhicitta is entirely dedicated to all sentient beings; such dedication of merit fills the realm of empty space and even exceeds it.
All the accumulations of merit belonging to all sentient beings are entirely transformed by the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva.

As the *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra* states: "The bodhisattva, having generated the bodhicitta, awakens to all phenomena; he knows that all phenomena are equal to the dharmadhātu, and that all phenomena come from nowhere, go nowhere, and cannot be known."

Nevertheless, by means of the wisdom that knows things as they are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), one realizes that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty, causing all sentient beings to likewise awaken to this realization.

If a bodhisattva generates the mind in this way, it is said to be the bodhisattva’s mind of enlightenment; the mind that seeks the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; the unsurpassed mind; the mind of great compassion and gentleness; the tireless mind of great pity; the non-regressing mind of great joy; the stainless mind of great equanimity; the mind of emptiness free from artificial activity; the tranquil mind of signlessness (*animitta*); and the wishless and non-abiding mind.
In this regard, one should ask:
how is it that a small root of virtue, when dedicated toward omniscience, does not become exhausted during the interval until one sits at the seat of enlightenment?
Answer: As stated in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"For example, suppose a single drop of water enters the great ocean; even until the end of the kalpa, it cannot be exhausted within that interval."
It is likewise with a bodhisattva’s dedication of even a small root of goodness toward omniscience; it cannot be exhausted from that point until they sit at the site of enlightenment.
The *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra* states: "There may be a bodhisattva who, upon seeing a person in poverty, gives rise to a heart of compassion and bestows even a small amount of rice.
As the Buddha has taught, this mind is vast and great, and is called the supreme gift."
How much more so regarding all dharmas that are bestowed; for although the gift itself may be small, the merit of the mind set upon omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) is immeasurable.

The *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* states that the Tathāgata Tārakarāja first resolved his mind on enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta. In the past, that Tathāgata Tārakarāja was a cowherd who, through the causal condition of offering *mucilinda* flowers, gave rise to this resolve.

The Tathāgata Yaśas first generated the mind of enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata Vidyutprabha. In the past, that Tathāgata Yaśas was a weaver; it was through the causal condition of offering a strand from the edge of a fine cotton cloth that he first generated this resolve.

The Tathāgata Arciṣmān first resolved his mind upon awakening in the presence of the Tathāgata Anantaprabha. In the past, that Tathāgata Arciṣmān was a city watchman; it was through the causal condition of offering a single grass lamp that he first generated this resolve.

The Tathāgata Duṣprasaha first resolved his mind upon awakening in the presence of the Tathāgata Dṛḍhapada. In a former life, that Tathāgata Duṣprasaha was a woodcutter; it was through the causal condition of offering a tooth-stick that he first gave rise to this resolve.

The Tathāgata Guṇaketurāja first resolved his mind upon bodhicitta in the presence of the Tathāgata Suvarṇanāman. In a former life, that Tathāgata Guṇaketurāja was a water-carrier; it was through the causal condition of offering a water vessel for drawing water that he first gave rise to this resolve.

The Tathāgata Balasena first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata Mahābhuja. In the past, that Tathāgata Balasena was a king of physicians; it was through the causal condition of offering a single āmalaka fruit that he first gave rise to this resolve.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "Suppose there were someone who, for the sake of seeking the fruit of arhatship, practiced generosity by filling boundless worlds with mani-jewels."

If there is a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, having seen this, gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy associated with omniscience, then the mass of merit resulting from that associated sympathetic joy, compared to the mass of merit from the previous gift, does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not even equal one *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part.
Question:
How is it that a bodhisattva can surpass the aforementioned generosity? Answer:
Because it is dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha said: "Śāriputra!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to surpass all the generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom cultivated by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) by generating a single mind of sympathetic joy associated with omniscience (sarvajñatā), taking great compassion as their precursor; it is only after this that bodhisattvas generate the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Therefore, one should know that the great bodhicitta is preceded by great compassion (mahākaruṇā). How is this to be known?
As the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "If bodhisattvas desire to seek enlightenment, they should take great compassion as their precursor."

Just as the life-faculty of a person is preceded by inhalation and exhalation, so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: within the Mahāyāna Dharma that they have gathered, they take great compassion as their precursor.

Furthermore, just as the wheel-treasure serves as the vanguard among all the treasures of a universal monarch (cakravartin), so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: among all the Buddha-dharmas, the mind of great compassion (mahākaruṇā) serves as the vanguard.
Furthermore, it is said that bodhisattvas constantly examine their own faults while protecting others' faults with a heart of compassion.
The *Aparājitajaya-paripṛcchā Mahāyāna Sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"O Householder!"

If bodhisattvas wish to achieve great enlightenment, they should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings; they should not produce attachment to their own bodies or lives, nor should they be attached to any articles of pleasure, including all wealth, grain, houses, wives, children, food and drink, clothing, vehicles, couches and seats, incense, flowers, and unguents. They should not be attached to any such things at all.
Why is this? Householder!
Many sentient beings give rise to attachment toward their bodies, lives, and so forth; because of this attachment, they extensively create sinful karma and fall into the evil realms.

Furthermore, if sentient beings, having given rise to great compassion, do not produce attachment to their bodies, lives, and so forth, they will—by virtue of this non-attachment—be born in the happy realms; moreover, they will be able to direct their minds toward all sentient beings and extensively practice acts such as giving, performing them in conjunction with all wholesome dharmas.
One who cultivates as a bodhisattva forms their body through great compassion.
How is this known? As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Good son! If bodhisattvas possess ten qualities, they are those whose bodies are formed by great compassion.
What are these ten?"

First, seeing all sentient beings oppressed by suffering—without rescue, without reliance, and without a refuge—one should, having seen them, resolve to attain great bodhicitta in order to act as their protector;
second, having resolved upon bodhicitta, one causes those sentient beings to achieve the realization of the Dharma;
third, according to the Dharma thus attained, one brings about great benefit for all sentient beings.
Fourth, to cause stingy sentient beings to abide in generosity;
fifth, if they have violated the precepts, to cause them to cultivate pure ethical discipline;
sixth, if they are full of anger and resentment, to cause them to abide in patience.
Seventh, for those with excessive indolence, they cause them to arouse diligence;
eighth, for those with excessive distraction, they cause them to cultivate meditative concentration;
ninth, for those who lack wisdom, they cause them to attain supreme insight.
Tenth, when all sentient beings are oppressed by extreme suffering, the Bodhisattva universally works to pacify and eliminate it, ensuring that it does not become an obstacle to their awakening.
These are called the ten dharmas.

The *Dhāraṇīśvararāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "A bodhisattva may see a class of sentient beings ensnared by craving, who develop attachment and infatuation toward their own wives, children, and kin; because they are bound by this craving, they do not attain self-mastery."

The Bodhisattva expounds the essential points of the Dharma as is appropriate, causing sentient beings to understand the fetters of craving and attain mastery over them; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or when he sees a class of sentient beings giving rise to a mind of anger and resentment, mutually harming one another and producing many faults, the Bodhisattva teaches them the essential points of the Dharma as appropriate, causing them to sever the fault of anger and resentment; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or, seeing a class of sentient beings who, being influenced by evil friends, distance themselves from virtuous friends and constantly commit sinful deeds, the Bodhisattva teaches them the essentials of the Dharma as appropriate, so that they may always draw near to virtuous friends and distance themselves from evil friends; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or, seeing a class of sentient beings who are excessively greedy and attached, lacking contentment, and far removed from sublime wisdom, the Bodhisattva teaches them the essential points of the Dharma as appropriate, causing them to sever their greed and attachment and give rise to sublime wisdom; this is because the Bodhisattva has given rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or when he perceives a class of sentient beings who deny karmic retribution and cling to the views of nihilism or eternalism, the Bodhisattva teaches them the essential Dharma as appropriate, causing them to enter into the profound dependent origination and understand all karmic activities; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or, seeing a class of sentient beings who, being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and delusion, cling to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, the Bodhisattva expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma as appropriate for them, causing their eye of wisdom to become pure and severing all views and attachments; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or, seeing a class of sentient beings who are addicted to the flavors of birth and death and cling to the five aggregates as if they were executioners, the Bodhisattva teaches them the essential points of the Dharma as appropriate, causing them to escape from all three realms; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or, seeing a class of sentient beings bound by the snares of Māra—clinging with attachment to both the pleasant and the unpleasant—the Bodhisattva teaches them the essential Dharma as appropriate, causing them to be liberated from the bonds of Māra’s snares and to sever the mind that dwells in attachment to the pleasant and the unpleasant; this is because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Or, seeing a class of sentient beings who have bolted the gate of nirvāṇa and opened the door to the evil realms, the bodhisattva teaches them the essential points of the Dharma as appropriate, causing them to open the gate of nirvāṇa and bolt the door to the evil realms; it is for the sake of giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings that the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

If there are those who disparage or slander the bodhisattva’s dharma of patience, and they give rise to a mind of deceit and arrogance that creates obstacles to the Dharma, desiring to cause the bodhisattva to distance himself from the dharma of patience, the bodhisattva should know that this is the arising of Māra’s work.
The *Sutra on the Dharma-Door of Entering the Seal through the Power of Faith* states that the Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were someone who created obstacles and hindrances to all the roots of goodness possessed by all sentient beings throughout all worlds, as numerous as the atoms within them; yet, suppose another person were to create obstacles to even a single root of goodness belonging to a single upāsaka who has no other teacher or master and who fully cultivates the ten virtuous actions. Such a transgression would be many times greater than the former, exceeding it by incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers."
Suppose there were someone who created obstacles for all the roots of goodness belonging to all the upāsakas in all worlds, as numerous as atoms;

yet if another person were to create obstacles for even a small root of goodness in a single bhikṣu, the sin of the latter would be many times greater than that of the former, by incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) multiples.
In this same sequence, [one should understand] those who follow by faith,
those who follow by dharma, the srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, the arhat, those on the stage of the eight persons, and the pratyekabuddhas;
as well as the bodhisattvas who travel by sheep-cart, the bodhisattvas who travel by elephant-cart, and those with the supernormal powers of the sun and moon.
If there were someone who created obstacles and hindrances to all the roots of goodness belonging to those bodhisattvas who practice the spiritual powers of śrāvakas,
or to those bodhisattvas who practice the spiritual powers of śrāvakas within all worlds as numerous as atoms;
yet, if there were another person who [created an obstacle] to even a single bodhisattva who practices the spiritual powers of a Tathāgata—
If one creates obstacles for even a single root of goodness, giving rise to a mind of deceit and arrogance and conceiving anger,
such a transgression is many times greater than the former incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Suppose there were someone who plucked out the eyes of all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of dust, and furthermore plundered all their means of livelihood and possessions; yet, if another person were to give rise to a mind of contempt and arrogance toward a single bodhisattva, becoming angry and resentful, reviling, slandering, and further harassing them, the sin of the latter would exceed that of the former by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) number.

If there should be someone who, toward a bodhisattva, gives rise to a mind of deceit and arrogance for whatever reason and becomes filled with anger, by virtue of this karmic offense they will fall into the Great Howling Hell. Their body will be five hundred *yojanas* in size and possess five hundred heads; each head has five hundred tongues, and each tongue is ploughed by five hundred plows amidst great, blazing flames.

Suppose there were someone who, toward all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, were to strike and hack them with swords and staves, and furthermore, were to plunder and seize all their means of livelihood and possessions; yet, if another person were to give rise to a mind of contempt and arrogance toward a bodhisattva, becoming angry and harboring malice and harm, the transgression of the latter would be many incalculable times (*asaṃkhyeya*) greater than that of the former.

Suppose there were a person who, having conceived an extremely evil mind and a mind intent on harming all sentient beings, were to kill every single Arhat in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and suppose they were further to destroy as many stupas and temples for the Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—those made of various jewels, adorned with jeweled railings, erected banners and pennants, and exquisitely decorated. Yet, if another person, toward a Bodhisattva who has resolved upon the Mahāyāna and planted the seeds of the Mahāyāna, should, for any reason whatsoever, give rise to a mind of deceit and arrogance, becoming angry, insulting, reviling, and further harassing them, the sin of the latter would be many times greater than that of the former, beyond measure (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Why is this? Because it is the Bodhisattvas who are able to give birth to all Tathāgatas, ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
Should anyone slander a Bodhisattva, they are thereby slandering the True Dharma.
If one slanders a bodhisattva, because there is no other dharma that can be taken up [as a refuge], it is only the dharma of a bodhisattva that can be taken up.

Suppose there were someone who gave rise to anger toward all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions; yet, if another person were to give rise to anger toward a bodhisattva and, having done so, abandon and turn their back on them, taking no pleasure in looking upon them, the transgression of the latter would be many times more severe than that of the former, by incalculable numbers (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Suppose there were someone who slaughtered all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and further plundered everything they possessed; yet if another person were to give rise to slander toward even a single bodhisattva, such a transgression would be many incalculable times (*asaṃkhyeya*) greater than the former.

The *Maitreya-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva were to give rise to anger, revile, and strike all sentient beings throughout a full trichiliocosm, that bodhisattva would nevertheless not be corrupted, ruined, harmed, or distressed."
If this bodhisattva, toward even a single bodhisattva, gives rise to a single thought of anger, however slight it may be, this bodhisattva is thereby fallen, lost, and afflicted.

Why is this? Because that single bodhisattva has, throughout so many eons, donned the armor of patience and never abandoned the mind of omniscience; therefore, this bodhisattva should not give rise to even a momentary anger toward him.

The *Mañjuśrī-vikrīḍita-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī, you should now know that what is called 'harm' refers to the distinct destruction and loss of roots of virtue accumulated and cultivated over a hundred eons; this is termed 'harm'."

A practitioner of the bodhisattva path should understand it thus: if one does that which is not beneficial toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, one incurs the retribution of great sin; whereas one who performs various beneficial acts obtains a great mass of merit.
The Treatise on the Essential Meaning of the Mahāyāna Jewel, Fascicle Two.
The Treatise on the Essential Meaning of the Mahāyāna Jewel, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu.
The *Samādhi-aniyata-mudrā-sūtra*, translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Dharma-pāla and others—

Great Masters of the Transmission of the Dharma (Chuánfàn Dàshī) who were granted the purple robe and served as Assistant Directors of the Court of State Ceremonial— states that the Buddha said: "O Mañjuśrī!"

Suppose there were someone who, throughout an entire eon, plucked out the eyes of all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions; and suppose there were a son or daughter of good family who, toward those aforementioned sentient beings, gave rise to a heart of compassion and restored their eyes to their former state for the duration of that same full eon.

Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there is someone who, having developed a pure mind toward a bodhisattva who has resolved upon the Mahāyāna, gazes upon them for even a single moment, such an accumulation of merit is many times greater than the former, being incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) in number.

Suppose there were someone who went throughout all the prisons of sentient beings in the ten directions and completely released them from their bonds, further enabling them to attain the supreme and exquisite happiness of a universal monarch or the Lord Śakra.

Mañjuśrī! If, moreover, there should be someone who, with a pure mind, gazes upon and praises a bodhisattva who has resolved upon the Mahāyāna through faith and understanding, such a mass of merit would be many times greater than the former, by an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).
The *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrāsūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!

If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were to practice universal giving toward all sentient beings in all worlds—equal in number to the most minute atoms—daily providing them with celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial exquisite garments."
Furthermore, if there is a person who, toward a single upāsaka who has no other teacher or honored one and who fully cultivates the ten wholesome actions, should give rise to this thought:
"This person is one who trains in the practice of the Buddha's precepts."
If one were to offer a single meal on a single day, the mass of merit resulting therefrom would be many times greater than the previous incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*).

Following this same sequence, if one were to provide double the offerings to each successive recipient—whether it be a single bhikṣu, a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), a follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), or even a pratyekabuddha—the merit would increase accordingly.

If there should be another person who merely sees a painted image of a Buddha, or an image of the Tathāgata within a scripture or a case, the mass of merit from such an act is many times greater than the preceding incalculable number; how much more so for one who joins their palms in respect, or makes offerings with flowers, incense, ointments, lamps, and a pure mind—the mass of merit from such acts is many times greater than the preceding incalculable number.

Furthermore, suppose there were someone who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, daily offered divine food of a hundred flavors and divine, exquisite garments to as many Buddha-Bhagavāns and their assemblies of śrāvakas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, thereby making offerings and providing sustenance.

Furthermore, if there is someone who, toward a bodhisattva practicing the sheep-cart vehicle—who has planted roots of goodness under whichever Buddha and is endowed with a pure mind—takes up that person and offers them a single meal for one day, such a mass of merit will be many times greater than the former incalculable number.

Suppose there were someone who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, daily offered and made offerings of celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial exquisite garments to as many bodhisattvas practicing the sheep-cart vehicle as there are atoms in all worlds.

Furthermore, if there is someone who, for a single day, gives a single meal to a bodhisattva who travels by means of an elephant chariot, the mass of merit from this is many times greater than the former incalculable number.

Suppose there were someone who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, daily offered celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial fine garments as alms and offerings to as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in all worlds, each traveling on elephant-drawn chariots.

If, moreover, there is a person who, at the place where a Bodhisattva practices the divine powers of the sun and moon, gives a single meal for the duration of one day, such a mass of merit is many times greater than the former incalculable number.

If there were someone who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, daily offered celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial, exquisite garments as alms and offerings to bodhisattvas possessing divine powers, equal in number to all the atoms within every world-system.

Furthermore, if there is another person who, for a single day, gives a single meal to a bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal powers of a śrāvaka, the mass of merit from this act will be many times greater than the former incalculable number.

Suppose there were someone who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, daily offered celestial food of a hundred flavors and celestial exquisite garments as alms and offerings to all those bodhisattvas who possess the spiritual powers of śrāvakas, equal in number to the atoms within all worlds.

If, moreover, there is someone who, for a single day, gives a single meal to a bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal powers of a Tathāgata, the mass of merit from this would be many times greater than the former incalculable number.
In this regard, one should ask:
what is meant by "bodhisattvas who travel by sheep-cart" up to "bodhisattvas who travel by the supernatural power of a Tathāgata"?
Answer:
As stated in the *Samādhi-aniyata-mudrā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:

"Mañjuśrī, there are five kinds of conduct for bodhisattvas, namely: the conduct of a sheep-cart, the conduct of an elephant-cart, the conduct of the sun and moon deities, the conduct of the śrāvakas, and the conduct of the Tathāgatas."
Among these, the two types of bodhisattvas—the sheep-cart practitioner and the elephant-cart practitioner—may regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

However, the three types of bodhisattvas—the sun-and-moon-vehicle practitioner, the śrāvaka-vehicle practitioner, and the Tathāgata-vehicle practitioner—shall no longer regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, what is it like for those bodhisattvas who travel by means of a sheep-drawn carriage?
It is, for example, as if there were a person who wished to pass through worlds as numerous as the atoms in five buddha-fields, and then thought to himself:
"I shall mount a sheep-drawn carriage."

Having made this resolve, he immediately mounted [the vehicle] and set out along the road; though he traveled for an exceedingly long time and endured great hardships over a distance of one hundred yojanas, he was suddenly blown back eighty yojanas by a mighty wind.
"Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
If this person were to ride that sheep-cart for even one kalpa, or even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, would they be able to traverse all those worlds, or even a single world?"
Mañjuśrī said: "No, World-Honored One."
"If one were able to surpass it, such a thing is impossible.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

It is so, it is so. There may be a bodhisattva who, having first generated the mind of great enlightenment, subsequently neither upholds nor recites the Mahāyāna teachings; instead, they take delight in practicing the Śrāvaka teachings and praise them accordingly, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining their meaning, and further causes others to uphold, practice, and understand them.
For this reason, their wisdom becomes dull and inferior, and they regress from the path of unsurpassed wisdom.

Although these bodhisattvas previously cultivated the root of wisdom and the eye of wisdom of the great bodhicitta, because their wisdom has become dull and inferior, they suffer loss and ruin; these are called bodhisattvas who travel by sheep-cart.
Who is called a person who is a bodhisattva traveling by elephant chariot?
It is like a person who wishes to traverse worlds as numerous as the atoms within the aforementioned buddha-fields, and then thinks to themselves:
"I shall mount a magnificent and excellent elephant chariot complete with its eight parts."
Having made this thought, he immediately mounted [the vehicle] and proceeded along the road.
After traveling two thousand yojanas over the course of a hundred years, he was suddenly blown back a thousand yojanas by a great wind.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Would such a person be able to traverse even a single world-system?
Mañjuśrī said: "No, World-Honored One."
"If one were able to surpass it, such a thing is impossible.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

It is so, it is so. There may be a bodhisattva who, having first generated the great mind of enlightenment, subsequently neither upholds nor recites the Mahāyāna teachings, but instead takes delight in practicing, upholding, reading, and understanding the Śrāvaka teachings; such a person is called a bodhisattva who travels by elephant chariot.
Who is called a person practicing the divine power of the sun and moon?

It is, for example, like a person who wishes to traverse as many worlds as there are atoms in the aforementioned Buddha-fields, and that person proceeds along the road by means of the divine power of the sun and moon.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Would such a person be able to traverse that many worlds?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Such a person would be able to pass through it, though the time would be exceedingly long and they would undergo diligent suffering throughout."
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī, it is so, it is so."

There may be a bodhisattva who, having first resolved upon great bodhicitta, takes no pleasure in practicing the teachings of the śrāvakas, nor does he even uphold or recite a single four-line verse from them; rather, he takes pleasure only in reading, reciting, explaining, and understanding the Mahāyāna teachings—this is called a person who practices the divine power of the sun and moon.
Who is called a bodhisattva who practices the supernatural powers of a śrāvaka?

It is, for example, like a person who wishes to traverse worlds as numerous as the atoms in the aforementioned buddha-fields, yet proceeds along the way by means of the supernatural powers of a śrāvaka.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Would such a person be able to traverse that many worlds?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This person is able to transcend it."
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī, it is so, it is so."

There may be a bodhisattva who, having already awakened the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), delights in practicing the Mahāyāna teachings; furthermore, they place their faith in, take refuge in, and draw near to other bodhisattvas who practice the Mahāyāna, resolve upon the Mahāyāna, recite the Mahāyāna, and uphold the Mahāyāna. They aspire to receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna, and even when encountering circumstances that threaten their very lives, they do not abandon the Mahāyāna for even a moment. Moreover, they honor and make offerings with incense, flowers, and the like to others who practice the Mahāyāna, and they do not give rise to arrogance toward bodhisattvas who have not yet studied it. This is called a bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal powers of a śrāvaka.
Who is called a bodhisattva who practices the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata?

It is like a person who wishes to pass through as many worlds as there are atoms in the aforementioned buddha-fields; such a person seeks the supernatural power of a Buddha and proceeds along the way.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Would such a person be able to traverse that many worlds quickly?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When such a person gives rise to this mind for even a single kṣaṇa, they are immediately able to swiftly traverse that many worlds."
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī, it is so, it is so."

There may be a bodhisattva who, having already generated the great bodhicitta and even attained a thorough understanding of the most supreme, profound, and vast principles of the Mahāyāna, constantly generates the great bodhicitta out of compassion to rescue and deliver all sentient beings; having applied diligent effort toward the six pāramitās and the four saṃgrahavastus, they further cause others to likewise abide therein—this is called a bodhisattva who practices through the supernormal powers of a Tathāgata.
In this regard, it should be said: if there are those who slander the True Dharma, they create obstacles and hindrances to the Dharma, which constitutes an extremely grave offense.

As the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There may be some who practice the Bodhisattva Vehicle and, although they have previously seen hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-Tathāgatas and have extensively practiced giving under those Buddhas up to the cultivation of wisdom, they give rise to the notion of a 'grasping mind' (*upalambha-saṃjñā*)."

Although they may go to the assemblies of the Buddhas to listen to and receive the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not give rise to respect; whether in body or mind, they are entirely impure. Giving rise to defiled wisdom, they commit great sinful karma and thereby slander the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Because they slander this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they thereby slander the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, as well as the all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) of the Buddhas; for this reason, it is said that they create a great obstacle and hindrance to the Dharma.

This continuity of karma causes one to fall into the great hells, where one remains for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years; emerging from one hell, one enters another, thus passing through successive cycles of formation and destruction. Having emerged from the hells, one further falls into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

These karmic offenses that obstruct the True Dharma will result in a continuous succession of births leading to rebirth in the five Avīci hells. Is it now possible to calculate the measure of these karmic offenses, or is it beyond description?"
The Buddha said, "Stop, Śāriputra!"
You should not say this.
Furthermore, there are many kinds of demonic activities for those practicing the bodhisattva path, as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Furthermore, Subhūti..."
If there is anyone who establishes various names, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
If Māra comes to the bodhisattva and speaks thus:
"This bodhisattva of yours has manifested perfect enlightenment and established these names."
At that time, the Bodhisattva should engage in investigation: if he abides in the signs of non-retrogression, then Māra and his heterodox followers will find no opportunity.

However, if he gives rise to a conceptualizing mind, thinking "I have received the prediction," he will immediately produce arrogance and treat other Bodhisattvas with deceit and pride. This is the skillful means of evil Māra intended to cause the Bodhisattva to distance himself from Prajñāpāramitā; being unguarded by virtuous friends and pursued by evil associates, he may fall to the stage of a Śrāvaka or the stage of a Pratyekabuddha. One who gives rise to such a mind associated with deceit and pride incurs a transgression far more grave than the four root offenses.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
The *Mañjuśrī-vikrīḍita-sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī said:
"O Devaputra!"
Whatever activities are performed to accomplish this, all are the deeds of Māra.
Whether there is something sought, something grasped, or something relinquished, all are the deeds of Māra.
If there is anything desired, anything imagined, anything experienced, or anything conceptualized, all these are the works of Māra.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If there is any attachment toward the bodhicitta, all such things are the work of Māra.
If there is any attachment toward the minds of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, all such things are the work of Māra.

Furthermore, giving that gives rise to pride, ethical discipline that dwells in discrimination, patience that engenders anger, diligence that consists of conceptual proliferation, meditative concentration that grasps at signs, and wisdom that involves mental fabrication—all these are the works of Māra.
If one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and delights in dwelling in tranquility, this is the work of Māra.
If one gives rise to a sense of intellectual understanding regarding the merits of fewness of desires, contentment, and the dhūta practices, this is the work of Māra.

Whether one practices emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of conceptual proliferation, or detachment, if one gives rise to the conceit of "I" regarding the practice taught by the Tathāgata and engages in discrimination, all such acts are the work of Māra.
"O Son of Heaven!
Even when conceptualization or non-conceptualization, seeing, hearing, perceiving, knowing, or the arising of mental conceptions occurs, all of these are the works of Māra.
The Son of Heaven asked:
“Mañjuśrī! From what causes do these various demonic activities arise?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
All demonic activities arise from association with the superior [defilements]. Why is this so?"
Furthermore, the various māras seek an opportunity within the teachings of superior application; if it were not for these supreme dharmas of application, what could the māras possibly do?
The Devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the bodhisattva’s superior correspondence?
What is non-correspondence? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!
If two dharmas are associated, this is precisely an association of predominance. Why is that?"

The conjunction of these two dharmas constitutes the basis for worldly union; this predominant conjunction is a synonym for "right conjunction," this right conjunction is a synonym for "non-conjunction," this non-conjunction is a synonym for "the absence of conceptual proliferation," and this absence of conceptual proliferation is a synonym for "right conjunction."
Whether in association or non-association, this is what is established therein.
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!

There is no association with the eye and no association with forms, and so on, up to no association with the mind and no association with phenomena; this is called the bodhisattva’s correct association.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
You should know that there are twenty kinds of dharmas by which bodhisattvas give rise to the works of Māra, causing Māra to become fierce and bold.
What are these twenty?

First, to approach, serve, and make offerings to those who are engaged in the practice for liberation, those who fear birth and death (*saṃsāra*), or those who practice superior yogic conduct through skillful means—all such acts are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Second, if one contemplates only emptiness while abandoning sentient beings, this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Third, if one contemplates only the unconditioned while becoming weary and indolent toward conditioned roots of goodness, this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Fourth, although one gives rise to a concentrated mind, one does not cultivate the practice of meditative concentration; this is a demonic activity of a bodhisattva.
Fifth, while the teacher of the Dharma delights in speaking, the listener does not give rise to great compassion; this is a demonic activity of a bodhisattva.
Sixth, to seek to practice giving toward those who possess precepts and virtue, while conceiving contempt and slander toward those who have broken their precepts, is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
Seventh, to delight in discoursing on the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas while concealing the teachings of the Mahāyāna is a Māra-activity of a bodhisattva.
Eighth, to conceal profound discourse while delighting in discoursing on discursive categories is a Māra-activity of a bodhisattva.
Ninth, although one knows the bodhisattva path, not seeking to cultivate the path of the *pāramitās* is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Tenth, using words that correspond to superior praise to instruct those sentient beings who do not correspond [to such praise] is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Eleventh, although one plants roots of goodness, to turn one's back on the bodhicitta is a demonic activity of a bodhisattva.
Twelfth, although one practices a continuous stream of corresponding contemplative exercises, to fail to instruct sentient beings as is appropriate is a demonic activity of a bodhisattva.

Thirteenth, although one seeks to exhaust those afflictions without remainder, yet feels revulsion and abandonment toward the afflictions that continue the cycle of birth and death—this is a Māra-affliction for a bodhisattva.
Fourteenth, although one further investigates with superior wisdom, yet does not take as an object of focus the sphere of great compassion—this is a Māra-affliction for a bodhisattva.
Fifteenth, if one does not possess skillful means regarding all virtuous practices, this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

Sixteenth, although one aspires to the Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, yet delights in receiving and upholding the scriptures of the Lokāyata and other non-Buddhist outsiders, this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Seventeenth, although one has heard much, one constantly keeps the teachings one has heard secret and begrudgingly refuses to let others know them; this is a demonic work of a bodhisattva.
Eighteenth, although one has heard much, one teaches and transmits them to others for worldly reasons, seeking to acquire wealth and profit from them; this is a demonic work of a bodhisattva.
Nineteenth: Not to approach, honor, or serve those Dharma masters who abide in the Mahāyāna;
instead, to praise those who abide in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—those who are not of the same class—is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.

Twentieth: When a bodhisattva, relying on his possession of wealth, majesty, and great prosperity—whether as Śakra, Brahmā, a World Protector (Lokapāla), a king, or a householder—does not associate with, respect, or serve others because of that very majesty and prosperity, this is a work of Māra for that bodhisattva.
These are the twenty kinds of dharmas of a bodhisattva that give rise to demonic activities and cause Māra to become fierce and bold.

The *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "If there is a bodhisattva who possesses great renown, wealth, power, and a noble lineage, and who has many attendants and is endowed with meritorious conduct—it is because of such things that they give rise to indolence, do not seek corresponding superior practices through wisdom, and become arrogant and heedless."

Or one may see a Bodhisattva who has perfected the renunciation of the household life, constantly seeking the Dharma of correspondence through the practice of wisdom; enduring toil and suffering, he is able to accept great winds and intense heat with equanimity, his flesh and blood wasting away until his appearance becomes haggard and unsightly.

Yet, when a bodhisattva, having seen such superior efficacy in another, gives rise to a sense of contempt and arrogance, refuses to listen to or accept their well-spoken words, and further increases his haughtiness and deluded pride—this constitutes being ensnared by the hook of a bodhisattva’s demonic power.

It is further said that there are four kinds of dharmas that act as obstacles and hindrances to the Mahāyāna: first, manifesting one's own virtues; second, concealing the virtues of others; third, the intense flourishing of pride; and fourth, the firm persistence of anger and resentment.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas should not consider the mere arousal of the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) as sufficient for contentment; rather, they should extensively cultivate the corresponding superior practices.
In this regard, one should ask:
what is the conduct of a lay bodhisattva?
Answer: As stated in the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Householder Śūra*, the Buddha said:
"Householder!"

Although a lay bodhisattva dwells within a household, they constantly cultivate the various deeds practiced by true practitioners (*saddharmicārin*). They do not perform those deeds that are not practiced by true practitioners; they enjoy things according to the Dharma and not contrary to it. They seek their livelihood through hardship and maintain themselves through right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), never living by wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) or causing distress to others. Although they constantly enjoy the benefits they have acquired, they give rise to the contemplation of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*). Extensively practicing giving with the true Dharma, they practice great renunciation without stinginess. They honor and serve their parents, and toward their wives, children, slaves, laborers, and even friends and acquaintances, they always instruct and guide them with the true Dharma.
Furthermore, what constitutes the improper conduct of a lay bodhisattva?
As stated in the *Sūtra on the Obstacles to Leaving Home*, the Buddha told the Venerable Mahānāma:

"You should now know that those who are born blind, deaf, or mute; those who are *śvapacas* (outcastes) and do not understand joy; those who are full of slander; those who are deceitful and crooked; those who are impotent; those who are constantly servants; those who undergo the transformation into a woman's body; and even camels, donkeys, pigs, dogs, and venomous snakes—beings such as these, from life to life and birth to birth, will not give rise to love or joy for the Buddha’s teaching."
Furthermore, Mahānāman!
If a lay bodhisattva possesses four kinds of qualities, these constitute difficult tasks.

First, regarding those sentient beings who have previously planted roots of virtue under past Buddhas, as well as those who seek liberation and those who delight in the mind of the Noble Path—if one creates obstacles or difficulties for them, this is the first difficult task for a lay bodhisattva.

Second, being greedily attached to wealth, treasures, children, and kinsmen, and thus lacking faith in the retribution of karma; if, when sons, daughters, wives, children, or other relatives and kin seek to renounce desire and leave the household life from within their wealth and status, one creates obstacles and difficulties for them—this constitutes the second difficult matter for a lay bodhisattva.

Third, a lay bodhisattva slanders the True Dharma; even though they may hear and receive teachings not previously heard, having heard them, they do not believe them but instead give rise to slander. This is the third difficult matter for a lay bodhisattva.
Fourth, to give rise to a mind of malice and various faults toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the virtue of precepts—this is the fourth difficult matter for a lay bodhisattva.
These four kinds, as well as the various other obstructive dharmas that arise individually, are all difficult matters for a lay bodhisattva throughout their successive births.
Suppose there is a person who has fallen into a foul, filthy well, and says to others:
"How wonderful this well is! It contains pure, clear water.
Upon hearing this, the other people perceive the foul water as clear water and do not regard it as impure.
