All sentient beings who are defiled by desire are likewise so: being themselves mired in the mud of desire, they further instruct others to become defiled as well; smelling foul odors themselves, they likewise instruct others to do the same; having themselves fallen into the perilous and difficult places of greed, hatred, and delusion, they further instruct others to fall therein as well.
Furthermore, it is like a person who captures an enemy and casts him into a fire-pit; this fire has fierce flames reaching seven times the height of a man, with neither fuel nor smoke.

Those who are stained by desire are just like this: they associate with women and praise the affairs of lust, falling themselves into the fire-pit of desire and further instructing others to fall as well. Once they have caused others to fall, those beings are constantly assailed by the afflictions of sickness, suffering, and distress.
Furthermore, it is like a person who instructs another to climb a mountain of sword-blades to experience pleasure, yet says:
"This mountain is level and free of precipices; you may climb it and enjoy your pleasure."

The affectionate attachment of worldly parents toward their children is likewise thus; because of their love for their children, they give rise to grasping and clinging toward the objects of sensual desire, yet the nature of such sensual desire is in fact profoundly evil, like a venomous serpent.
With a defiled mind, this person speaks of sensual matters with flattering words before his wife;
likewise, he uses flattering words to falsely describe as virtuous those three evil realms of extreme peril and terror.
Those who speak thus shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
*Mahāyāna-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā-śāstra*, Fascicle Three;
*Mahāyāna-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla,
Dharma-transmitting Master and Imperially Conferred Purple-Robed Śramaṇa,
Subject [Dharmapāla], and others, by imperial decree, based on the *Sūtra of the Questions of King Divākara*. As the Buddha said therein:
"Great King!

Those people who are stained by desire are attached to sensual matters and delight in seeing women practicing the ways of lust. They do not delight in approaching śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the precepts; rather, they harbor contempt for those endowed with virtuous conduct. Consequently, they diminish and lose all such qualities as faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom."

Because that foul gateway is filled with noxious vapors and overflowing with impurities, one gives rise to attachment and defilement; failing to feel revulsion or rejection, one dwells within that filth, becoming no different from maggots and other such creatures, devoid of shame and remorse, causing the extinction of the Dharma of devas and humans, and bringing ruin to body and life—this is what the wise censure and loathe.
Overpowered by those women, he becomes their servant;
taking as his nourishment impure substances such as saliva and flowing mucus, within that state of impurity he conducts himself in common with cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, foxes, and donkeys.

Those who distance themselves from filial piety and affection toward their parents, as well as toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and whose pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha has diminished, shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

On the perilous and terrifying shore, they climb the iron-fork tree and fall into the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci great hells; all this is because they were constantly preoccupied with such matters as intimacy with female companions, longing, laughter, play, amusement, singing, dancing, and performing as courtesans, and thus failed to give rise to thoughts of renunciation.

Furthermore, they do not reflect that their parents’ act of giving birth was exceedingly difficult; for ten months they carried them in their wombs, enduring all manner of hardships with total acceptance as impurities flowed forth.
Once he has been born, the various matters of suffering and affliction further increase; [the parents] nourish, cherish, and protect him with breast milk and loving care.
When he reaches adulthood, they instruct him in the various occupations of Jambudvīpa, desiring that their son obtain peace, security, benefit, and happiness.
At that time, his parents, desiring to bring their son peace and happiness, selected a wife from a noble family for him to marry.
Once the wife had arrived at the home, the son conceived a deep attachment to her; he became infatuated, immersed in passion, bound by craving, and mentally distressed.
Because he was attached to his wife and family, he failed to honor or provide for his parents with filial piety; instead, he treated them with contempt and abandoned them.
Later, when his parents grew old and infirm, their faculties weakened and they were in great need, the son devised a scheme to have them leave the house.
The Buddha said:
"Great King!

Observe that person who lacks a heart of compassion, gives rise to a mind of abandonment, and conceives a mind of harm, failing to consider how difficult it was for his parents to give him birth and raise him."
Yet those parents constantly performed acts of peace and happiness for their child, employing skillful means to cherish and protect them so that they might attain security.

But that child, in betrayal of their kindness, sent his parents away from his home; he then gathered constantly in joyful company with his wife and children, enjoying food, drink, clothing, and other necessities as he pleased.
By reason of these causes and conditions, they abandon the happy realms and practice such unrighteousness, and will certainly fall into the various evil destinies.
Furthermore, it is taught that all sentient beings alike engage in unwholesome conduct, which the Bodhisattvas alone do not practice—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth.
Having acted in this way, one will certainly obtain undesirable fruits.
As a verse in the *Samādhirāja Sūtra* says:
"The fool is addicted to various sensual matters, Cultivating intimacy with women of defiled and impure bodies."
One shall return to that state of defilement, falling into the various evil realms according to one's karma.
The Buddha does not praise or speak of matters of defiled desire, nor does he permit approaching women;
they are entangled by the ropes of great terror, for the ropes of lustful women are exceedingly firm and evil.
The fierce blaze of desire should be kept far away; the wise should know it to be like the venom of a malignant serpent.
Women possess no trustworthiness and cannot be relied upon; the wise should awaken to this path.
One should contemplate the supreme path of bodhi, which is that which the Buddhas of the past have personally approached;
having contemplated it, the noble path of bodhi becomes perfected, and one attains the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas.
As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*: "Among all the sinners within the various hells, the hell-wardens daily instruct them repeatedly, saying:

'You sinners have yourselves created evil karma; it shall certainly not fail its fruit. In accordance with the countless kinds of unwholesome karmic actions you committed, you now undergo countless kinds of suffering.'"
Because their causal characteristics are identical, there is no difference in the taking of the fruit; because they are like seeds, the same applies to the experiencing of the fruit.

For this reason, you sinners have now fallen into the Great Hell of Intense Heat; because the causes of your own unwholesome karma were fully accumulated in the past, the fruits of that unwholesome karma are likewise fully experienced here and now.
Thus, for a hundred thousand years, they committed sinful karma while in the Land of No Death, having no desire for benefit or happiness.
Then, as those sinners undergo their retribution until the fruits of hell are exhausted, they may be temporarily released and immediately seek protection.

From afar, the sinner sees a multitude like a vast, dark, and boundless cloud of great ferocity and immense power—resembling a pack of large, evil dogs with diamond-like muzzles—approaching and surrounding him with a terrible roar; having seen them, the sinner flees in all four directions.

Immediately, various dogs come forward and seize the sinner, devouring him at will; his skin and flesh are torn to shreds, his tendons and veins are severed and destroyed, and his limbs and joints are all separated from one another, until every part of his body has been devoured without remainder, not even as much as a mustard seed left behind.
Having eaten in this manner, sustained by the power of karma, they are born again and again; thus, through the long succession of time, they are once more devoured.
Such instances of karmic retribution are said to arise because one took the flesh of living beings by killing them; such is the fruit of harming sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the karmic retribution for the act of stealing: although that sinner sees the reality of the fruits of his actions, he is deluded by the illusions of evil karma and pursues them without understanding, thus seizing the wealth of others and taking possession of it as his own.

Because of this sin, the hell-wardens seize the offender; having seized him, they immediately take up sharp blades to cut off and sever his limbs and joints, and once severed, these parts are joined back together again.

Seeing other sinners, they all likewise flee; however, the hell-wardens each seize them, using either sharp swords, śaktis, or tomara-spears, or else pestles, all of which are ablaze with flames, to inflict various punishments such as hacking, cleaving, and beating.
All of these are the results of unwholesome karma from practicing the act of stealing.

They remain in this hell for countless hundreds of thousands of years; only after the karmic retribution for their theft has been exhausted, scattered, and brought to its ultimate limit will they be released.

Furthermore, the fruit of sexual misconduct is proclaimed as follows: those who are stained by desire see that woman in the Hell of the Ash River (Kṣāranadī), either floating or sinking, crying out in terror; that hell is ablaze with fierce and terrible flames, appearing like a flowing torrent.
Then that woman, weeping with grief and wailing aloud, called out to the man, saying:
"I myself created this karma; now I have fallen into this most perilous and evil place, the Hell of the Ash River, where there is no rescue and no refuge."
"Please grant us protection!
At that time, the lustful man, having heard the woman's cries of lamentation, was deluded by the illusions of karma and immediately rushed into that river.

Once this person has entered, the flowing flames touch their body, causing it to melt and disintegrate throughout until not even a remnant the size of a mustard seed remains; yet, sustained by the power of karma, they immediately come back to life again.

Furthermore, as before, he saw that woman crying out for help within the river of ashes; upon seeing her, the man also rushed forward to seize her. At that moment, the woman instead seized the man and struck him with a blazing iron club. Struck by the club, the man’s entire body was covered in blood and shattered until not even a fragment the size of a mustard seed remained.

Sustained by the power of their karma, those people who were lustful immediately return to life; because the cause of their lust was so heavy, they again rush forward to seize women. They remain together within the Great Hell of the Ash River for countless hundreds of thousands of years, until finally the karmic fruit of their lust is exhausted and dispersed to its ultimate limit, whereupon they are released.
Furthermore, one is born again, as explained at length in the sūtra.
In this regard, it should be understood that one must not give rise to attachment toward wealth or lifespan; for one who gives rise to attachment is practicing erroneously.
As stated in the *Rāstrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Great King!

For example, suppose in this world a man or a woman, while dreaming, sees a delightful garden or a delightful mountain, or sees a crowd of people in a bustling marketplace; yet upon waking, none of these exist at all."
"Great King!

It is also like a grove of various fruit trees, whose trunks, branches, and leaves are initially lush and green, gradually turning red; they successively form buds and then bloom, and not long after the flowers open, they immediately bear fruit. Once the fruit falls and begins to wither, it is seen to decay until, as before, neither flower nor fruit remains at all."
Now, Great King, you are likewise in this regard.

All the pleasures possessed by worldly kings—the joy of royal prosperity, the joy of the five royal sensual desires, as well as extensive elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; granaries, treasuries, wealth, and grain; palaces, gardens, and groves; gold, silver, and precious jewels; ministers, officials, and administrators; queens, concubines, and palace attendants; boys and girls; and even all members of the royal lineage—whatever such things there may be, you must abandon them all and seek liberation.

All these are entirely impermanent; they are unstable, non-ultimate, subject to change, unreal, and not long-lasting. They are shifting and wavering, disintegrating moment by moment; they are ultimately sinful, exhaustible, and subject to cessation. Reaching their final limit, they are phenomena of decay and loss, sources of fear and affliction that give rise to much sorrow and suffering; they are ruinous and falling away, severed and shattered, and phenomena of dispersal.
"Great King!
You should know it is just like this.

Furthermore, suppose four great mountains were to come from the four directions—mountains that are solid, unbreakable, and without flaw, with sublime peaks perfectly rounded—and were to fall simultaneously from the midst of space onto the earth; at that time, all sentient beings upon the great earth, as well as all forests, trees, grasses, and shrubs, would be utterly destroyed."

All these sentient beings, as well as grasses, trees, and the like, are unable to avoid it; even if they possessed power and strength, they could not flee, nor do they possess any skillful means or active functions by which to prevent it.
"Great King!

It is likewise with these four great terrors that come one after another; all sentient beings are unable to avoid them. Even if they possess power and influence, they cannot flee from them, nor is there any skillful means or action by which they can be averted."
What are the four? Great King!

When the fear of old age arrives, it destroys the appearance of youth; when the fear of illness arrives, it destroys the state of well-being; when the fear of death arrives, it destroys and extinguishes life; when wrong conduct arises, it destroys and causes one to lose right conduct.
Great King!
Furthermore, it is like the lion, the king among beasts; when he enters a herd of animals to seize one for food, he does so according to his desire without any difficulty.

"However, although that lion possesses great strength, once it enters the mouth of the great and wicked flying bird Mīṇa, it will find itself utterly helpless; the bird will devour it entirely, leaving nothing behind.
Great King!"

The arrow of death that strikes a person is likewise: one who is struck by this arrow becomes utterly bewildered and confused, with no rescue and no refuge. As the limbs are about to be severed and the flesh and blood wither away, one is oppressed by the torment of thirst; the facial features become terrifying, the hands and feet tremble, and one is rendered powerless and incapable. Saliva and mucus flow, and one is defiled by the impurities of excrement and urine. The various consciousnesses of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind cease to function; the throat and neck are constricted so that one cannot speak. Physicians abandon such a person as incurable—how then could they take any nourishment from various flavors of food and drink?
At that time, this person, driven by the power of their own karma, is about to rush toward another realm of existence.

Since beginningless time, they have been subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, circulating and revolving in saṃsāra without ceasing. When this consciousness abandons its current state and returns to depend upon another consciousness, the remaining karma of this life again takes up a physical body.
The jailers of Yama are most terrifying; one constantly treads within that long night of darkness.
When the consciousness is about to depart, the inhalations and exhalations gradually become faint and subtle; one is left alone without a companion, with nothing whatsoever to rely upon.

Once this realm has passed away, one immediately proceeds to another realm; alone one wanders upon a long and vast road, giving rise to extreme terror in a place of great fear. Traveling along deep and hidden paths, one enters a state of great darkness and peril, drowning in the great ocean of the long-flowing stream of birth and death. Blown by the winds of karma, one drifts without stability, unable to distinguish the directions or know where one is going; at that time, there is no rescue and no refuge.
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
Only the wholesome dharmas shall, at that time, be your refuge and your protection."
"Great King!
In this world, phenomena such as wealth and pleasure are ultimately unattainable; do not give rise to attachment toward them.
Whatever actions one performs are all erroneous conduct; therefore, Great King, you should cultivate correct conduct."

Regarding what is called "right conduct," as stated in the "Chapter on Reality": "If a king practices eight kinds of mental orientations, this constitutes the protection of the world in accordance with the True Dharma."

What are these eight? First, regarding those in the world who are childless and destitute, one should conceive of them as one’s own children. Second, regarding evil associates, one should regard them with care as if they were patients. Third, upon seeing those who suffer, one should give rise to the thought of rescuing and delivering them. Fourth, upon seeing those who possess happiness, one should give rise to the thought of rejoicing. Fifth, regarding all enemies, one should contemplate their conditions and give rise to the thought of being free from faults toward them. Sixth, regarding all virtuous friends, one should give rise to the thought of following and protecting them. Seventh, upon seeing various riches and pleasures, one should regard them as if they were medicine. Eighth, regarding one’s own body, one should cultivate the thought of impermanence.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Pāpabuddhibhañjana-sūtra*: "If a king can be fully endowed with four qualities, he should receive the royal consecration; he will then attain the dharma of non-retrogression, swiftly gain the affectionate regard of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and obtain vast wealth, happiness, and all-encompassing prosperity."

What are the four? First, to protect and uphold the Tathāgata’s teachings so that they may endure for a long time; second, to abandon sinful and unwholesome dharmas; third, to embrace the dharma-gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and fourth, to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In this context, what constitutes the abandonment of sinful and unwholesome dharmas?
As stated in the *Sūryagarbha-parivarta*, the Buddha said:
"Great King!"

In future ages, various kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras will completely seize from those who practice the True Dharma all their dwellings, fields, gardens, slaves, bedding and seating, medicines for illness, and even their four-legged animals; having thus taken all such things, they will either use them themselves or give them to others to use.
These kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras will obtain twenty kinds of undesirable conditions in this very life.
What are these twenty?
First, being abandoned by the noble and holy ones; second, being subjected to slander and defamation wherever one goes;
third, being estranged from friends and loved ones; fourth, frequently engendering enmity and resentment; fifth, having all material wealth and possessions utterly destroyed;
sixth, frequently giving rise to mental distraction; seventh, having physical deformities and deficiencies; eighth, [not...]
1. One falls into sleep; 2. one is constantly oppressed by the torment of thirst;
3. there is poison within one's drink; 4. friends treat one with contempt; 5. one is constantly at strife with others; 6.
the commands of one’s parents, wife, children, servants, and kinsmen are not carried out; 7. one’s own secret dharmas and secrets [are revealed].
Fifteenth, he reveals his wealth to others; sixteenth, he tells others all his secrets and private matters;
seventeenth, his wealth and possessions are squandered and dispersed among five parts; eighteenth, severe illnesses and afflictions come to oppress him;
nineteenth, those who provide him with medical care and medicine all abandon him.
Nineteenth, their flesh and blood will wither and dry up as they undergo various sufferings; twentieth, their bodies will be defiled by the flow of excrement and urine until they die.
Great King!

These twenty kinds of unpleasant phenomena will certainly and swiftly be experienced in this very life; they all result from the fact that those who practice the Dharma correctly were deprived by others of their resources and requisites for enjoyment, whether those resources were used by the practitioners themselves or given to others.

Due to these causes and conditions, after their lives have ended, they shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell, where for the duration of an entire kalpa they will drink molten copper out of thirst, swallow iron balls out of hunger, and wear garments of fire, thus undergoing various kinds of great and terrible suffering.

Having exhausted the lifespan of that eon, they emerge from hell and are reborn once again within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta). They dwell in vast wildernesses, places of extreme evil, peril, and parched desolation, where fierce, blazing hot winds blow from the four directions. The ground is hard and sharp, like the edge of a blade; there they undergo the sufferings of that realm for countless hundreds of thousands of years.

Thereafter, for a short time, or once that has ceased, they become a single mass of flesh in the great ocean, measuring one hundred yojanas; due to the causes of their past karma, they cause the entire area of one hundred yojanas within that ocean to become glowing, heated molten copper.
Thus, for many hundreds of thousands of years, they undergo the sufferings of hell within the great ocean.

Once that period has ended, they return here to this most evil, perilous, and vast wilderness, where they transform into lumps of flesh as large as mountains. Blown from all four directions by blazing winds, predatory birds and beasts from every quarter come to devour them. After a long time has passed, they may briefly cease to exist there, only to be reborn once again within the great hells.
Once the hellish retributions have ceased, they undergo these great fruits of evil suffering again and again; only after a full kalpa has passed do they finally obtain a human body.
Though born within a Buddha-land, they are fully possessed of the five turbidities and utterly devoid of wisdom; their eyes are squinted and they are further deaf and mute.
"Great King!
All such instances as these arise because those who practice the Dharma correctly have been robbed of their requisites for enjoyment and use.
As stated in the *Candraloka-parivarta*: 'O noble ones!'"
The great offenses committed by those who have gone forth within my Dharma are the extremely unwholesome karmas, namely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech.

That is to say, those kṣatriya kings, down to the officials of provinces, cities, and villages, extensively practice prohibitions against renunciants regarding their countries, provinces, cities, residences, and monasteries, not allowing them to dwell there; or they employ verbal subjugation, meaning harsh words of reproach and defamation, or physical subjugation, meaning the infliction of flogging and punishment.
Cycling through all those places in this manner, they find no liberation; having suffered decline and loss within the realms of gods and humans, they shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell.

At that time, all the great assemblies who had gathered, from the devas down to the kaṭapūtanas, gave rise to the most supreme and pure mind toward the Triple Gem. With various signs of profound respect, they spoke these words in unison:
"From this day forward, we vow to act as guardians within the teachings of all the World-Honored Ones."

All bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—even those who have broken the Buddha’s precepts, or those within the Buddha’s Dharma who do not maintain the practice of the precepts, but who have merely shaved their hair and beards and wear the kāṣāya robe, even if they are unrestrained—we shall conceive of them as our Great Teacher and provide protection for all, sustaining and supporting them with every necessary provision.

Furthermore, in whatever regions there may be officials who subject those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the *kāṣāya* to various forms of corporal punishment and flogging, we shall not provide them with protection and shall abandon all matters within their jurisdiction.

Should there arise in that kingdom various instances of flattery, deception, falsehood, strife, slaughter, pestilence, famine, invasion by foreign armies, untimely winds, rains, droughts, or floods, or the destruction of seeds—should such afflictions as these occur, we shall not bring about their cessation.
"We shall go to where there are disciples of the Buddha in other lands and provide them with protection; we shall then empty this realm and depart from it."
As stated in the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Kṣitigarbha!
In the past, there was a country named Pañcāla, and its king was named Jayasena."
At that time, there was a person subject to execution who, for the sake of preserving his life, secretly shaved off his hair and beard and wrapped a fragment of a *kāṣāya* robe around his neck.
Then the executioners bound the culprit at five points, drove him away, and cast him into the great wilderness of the Tailteka-vaṅga forest before returning.

That very night, in that desolate forest, a rākṣasī named Akṣamālā arrived with five thousand attendants. Suddenly seeing the man bound at the five limbs, with his hair and beard shaved off and wearing a fragment of a kāṣāya robe, she immediately circumambulated him to the right, prostrated before him, and departed from the forest.

Next, a rākṣasī named Khadirakaṇṭhā arrived with a retinue of one thousand; next, a rākṣasī named Karālakesī; and next, a rākṣasī named Khaḍgamukhī. They entered the forest one after another and each saw that person with his hair and beard shaven and wearing a fragment of a kāṣāya robe. Upon seeing this, although they were each driven by intense hunger, they did not dare to devour him; instead, they prostrated themselves and departed.

Furthermore, in the past there was a king named Most Victorious Merit (*Puṇyavara*). He had a wise minister who, according to the law, handed over a person deserving of execution to a drunken elephant.

This man had secretly draped a fragment of a saffron robe over his body; at that time, the drunken elephant raised its trunk and seized the criminal by both calves, exerting all its strength and power as it sought to hurl him to the ground.

At that time, the elephant saw the sinner’s body draped with a fragment of the crimson *kāṣāya*. Upon seeing him, he immediately conceived a pure mind; he then gently set the sinner upon the ground, knelt prostrate before him, weeping and repenting his transgressions, and further rubbed and washed the sinner’s two feet with his trunk.
The Buddha said:
"Kṣitigarbha!

Observe that elephant; although it has received the body of an animal in an unfavorable rebirth, when it saw someone wearing even a fragment of the kāṣāya, it was still able to abandon its course and depart, refraining from committing sinful deeds."

Furthermore, in future ages there will be *caṇḍāla* kings and their officials, as well as among śramaṇas, brahmins, and elders, those who are *caṇḍālas*, who are fundamentally ignorant yet give rise to pride in their supposed intelligence; they deceive the world with crooked speech, claiming, "I am one who seeks the unsurpassed Mahāyāna."

Those foolish outcastes (caṇḍāla), neither fearing nor considering the retribution of future lives, seek out faults through various means against those who have gone forth in my Dharma, whether they be vessels for the Dharma or not.
That is to say, they revile him with harsh words, inflict physical punishment upon his body, and restrict all the resources necessary for his livelihood.

Furthermore, they impose regulations upon various worldly activities; whether by observing his slowness or spying on his service, they seek out faults and establish restrictions, even going so far as to desire to take his life.

Those people will give rise to extreme transgressions toward all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of time; they shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell, severing their roots of goodness and incinerating their mental continuity, and are forever shunned by all those of wisdom.

The Treatise on the Essential Meaning of the Mahāyāna Jewel, Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the *Śramaṇa* Dharma-pāla and others, Great Masters of the Transmission of the Dharma (*Chuanfan*), recipients of the purple robe and junior ministers of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Shaoqing*). As stated in the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*: Furthermore, there may be those who are *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas*, up to and including *gṛhapati-cāṇḍālas*, who—regarding monasteries, groves, pavilions, and towers built for the Saṅgha of the four quarters, as well as provisions such as fields, lands, and attendants, or food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine; or flower trees, fruit trees, dyeing trees, incense trees, and shade trees, or even various articles of utility—if they themselves seize them, or incite others to seize them; or if they themselves enjoy them, or cause others to enjoy them.
Toward those who have gone forth within my Dharma, they may give rise to anger, or further revile, obstruct, suppress, and insult them;
they create hindrances to the True Dharma and incite disturbances against the teachers of the Dharma.
All of these constitute extreme transgressions against all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of time, and are even avoided by all those who possess omniscience.
Furthermore, regarding this matter, the World-Honored One has spoken thus:
"I grant permission for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) to receive the consecration of a Kṣatriya king and to enjoy wealth and prosperity."
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the consecration received by a Kṣatriya king, if he is not a bodhisattva who has attained forbearance, into what evil destiny would he fall?"
The Buddha said:

"Vajragarbha! If it is not a bodhisattva who has attained patience, yet is able to cultivate and accumulate the ten paths of wholesome action, and receives the consecration of a kṣatriya king as well as the enjoyment of wealth and prosperity, I also permit this."
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who have not attained forbearance (*kṣānti*) and have not fully cultivated the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), yet those *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings cause this profound teaching of the World-Honored One to decline and perish, they shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell. How can such individuals attain liberation?"
The Buddha said:

"Good son, one who has received the consecration of a Kṣatriya king, if they don the firm armor of the power of faith, generating vast pure faith within the Triple Gem; furthermore, if they do not slander my Dharma of renunciation of the three vehicles, nor even slight or disparage it down to a single four-line verse;

and if they do not disturb or harass those among the community who maintain the precepts or violate them, nor even those members of the bhikṣu-saṃgha who, though not having received the pure precepts, have merely shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya—[such a person shall attain this samādhi]."

Whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to individuals, one shall never encroach upon or seize any of their requisites or possessions. One shall constantly listen to and receive the sublime Dharma of the three vehicles that leads to liberation; according to what has been heard, one shall practice to the best of one's ability. One shall always draw near to those bhikṣus who practice the three vehicles, maintaining firm resolve and never giving rise to thoughts of opposition. One shall teach the Mahāyāna Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to enter it and further causing them to abide therein.
If there is a Kṣatriya king who is able to possess such characteristics, he should enjoy vast wealth and pleasures without falling away.
All the Tathāgatas of former Buddhas have granted their approval for this, and I now likewise grant my approval for this matter.
Furthermore, it is stated therein:

"If there should be a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king, or even a truly virtuous householder, whether in the present or in future ages, up until the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, they shall provide protection for themselves and others. They shall firmly guard and protect the pure teaching of the Buddha; furthermore, they shall protect those who abide in the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Mahāyāna—those individuals (pudgala) who have fully cultivated the virtue of pure precepts and possess great merit, whether they are vessels of the Dharma or not—even down to those who have merely shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya robe."

Furthermore, in order to protect and maintain the property belonging to stupas and monasteries, he shall not seize or encroach upon it—whether for his own use or to give to others—and shall immediately restrain anyone else who does so.
Such a mass of merit is immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond limit.
At that time, all the lords of the devas in the assembly, down to the lord of the piśācas, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"

If there should be a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king, or even a truly virtuous householder, who is endowed with such merits as these, we shall all provide protection for them and cause them to possess ten kinds of increasing matters.
What are the ten? First, the increase of lifespan;

second, the increase of freedom from calamities; third, the increase of freedom from illness; fourth, the increase of retinue; fifth, the increase of wealth and goods; sixth, the increase of requisites; seventh, the increase of mastery; eighth, the increase of reputation; ninth, the increase of virtuous friends; and tenth, the increase of wisdom.

We, together with our own retinues, shall always protect that truly virtuous Kṣatriya king; throughout his entire realm, we shall cause him to remain far removed from ten kinds of things and provide him with protection.

What are these ten? First, the enemy armies of other nations; second, the enemy armies of one's own nation; third, those who commit sinful deeds; fourth, those who commit murder and slaughter; fifth, untimely rain; sixth, malicious winds, violent storms, and extreme heat; seventh, most malevolent planetary influences (*nakṣatra*); eighth, famine; ninth, sudden illness and premature death; tenth, wrong views.
The *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:

"If there are devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others who act as protectors within my teaching, they are great donors who cause my Dharma-eye to endure for a long time and ensure that the lineage of the Triple Gem is neither severed nor interrupted. They provide protection for those born from my own mouth—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās born through transformation by the Dharma—as well as other sons and daughters of good family with pure faith, and even those who seek the Dharma of the ultimate truth or seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

I now personally entrust this to you—the great donors such as devas, nāgas, and yakṣas—as well as to Maitreya and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa; you shall provide protection in accordance with my instructions.
If one wishes to dwell securely in the practice of the True Dharma, one will immediately attain excellence of mind.
How does one attain excellence of mind?
As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, a bodhisattva attains excellence of mind.
In this context, what is meant by "excellent mind"?
It means that if one can become detached from body and mind, one attains excellence of mind.
One should give rise to such a thought and examine it with careful scrutiny:
By what means does my mind proceed?
Furthermore, by what is it called "wholesome"?

If one proceeds in what is wholesome, the mind becomes pure through joy; because of this mental joy, one proceeds in the wholesome, thereby giving rise to manifold disenchantment and manifold investigation, whereby all unwholesome states are completely severed and extinguished.
The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas should not give rise to such thoughts.

If a thought arises, all evil Māras will find an opportunity to exploit it; the Buddhas and Tathāgatas will not rejoice in it, the noble ones will not feel joy, and one's own portion of roots of goodness will likewise diminish and be lost."

Furthermore, if one gives rise to the thought that nothing is actually produced, then all evil Māras will find no opportunity to exploit them; all Buddhas and Tathāgatas will likewise cherish and delight in them; the hearts of the worthy and holy ones will rejoice; and their own portion of roots of goodness will not diminish or be lost.
If he practices in this manner, he gives rise to the mind in all places.
As that mind arises, he turns the wheel of Dharma, and the teachings he proclaims are free from confusion or disorder.
As stated in the *Cittaviveka-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "Maitreya!

If bhikṣus speak in a confused and disordered manner, although they may possess great learning, it will instead give rise to arrogance, delusion, and forgetfulness; their inner minds will be distracted and lack concentration."

That crooked mind arises in continuous succession, causing one to distance oneself from śamatha and vipaśyanā; one is not respected by others, nor do devas, nāgas, and yakṣas accord with them, and the right practices they cultivate do not reach fulfillment.
If one finds nothing at all within that which is practiced, this is called right practice.
If one wishes to understand what this right practice is, it refers precisely to diligently practicing the cultivation of much learning and seated meditation.

Furthermore, it is stated therein: "If there were a bodhisattva who diligently practiced sublime conduct as a leader and constructed wonderful stupas made of the seven precious gems that filled the trichiliocosm, I would still not grant my approval to such a person."
Furthermore, if there is anyone who hears and receives even a single four-line verse of the true Dharma that accords with the Prajñāpāramitā, I shall hold them in high esteem and praise them.
Why is this? For extensive learning can give rise to the bodhi of all Buddhas, which in turn arises from non-attachment within the world.
If there is a bodhisattva who diligently cultivates superior practices as a leader, they should preach and instruct the Dharma for others.

When a bodhisattva, through their teaching, causes others not to give rise to attachment toward phenomena that provoke attachment, the mass of merit they acquire becomes vast and immeasurable, and their karmic obstructions are dissolved.

Maitreya! Suppose there were bodhisattvas throughout Jambudvīpa who have diligently practiced superior conduct and lead others; if they were all to serve and make offerings to a single bodhisattva who diligently practices the preaching and exposition of the Dharma; and suppose there were bodhisattvas throughout Jambudvīpa who diligently practice the preaching and exposition of the Dharma, and they were all to serve and make offerings to a single bodhisattva who diligently practices meditative seclusion—the Buddha permits and rejoices in such deeds as these.
Why is this? Because the activity of wisdom is the most supreme among all difficult activities; it is preeminent and most excellent throughout the entire triple world.
Furthermore, regarding the practitioner who proclaims the True Dharma, as stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the Buddha said:

Kāśyapa! It is like a merchant leader who, wishing to enter the great ocean to seek priceless jewels, first carefully inspects a sturdy ship or raft, and having reached the place where the jewels are found, returns again to his own home.

Kāśyapa! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to enter the ocean of omniscience: first, they must observe and diligently practice the six pāramitās, until they transcend all stages of foolish ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, and only then abide in the state of the Buddha-fruit.
The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"Great King!

The root of the mind of omniscience is never severed; one should arouse diligence and exert oneself in instructing others regarding this very root. One should practice giving without weariness, because it is dedicated toward the wisdom of omniscience."
One never tires of upholding the precepts, because one dedicates them for the sake of all sentient beings;
one never tires of practicing patience, because one seeks the physical marks of a Buddha;
one never tires of practicing diligence, because one zealously cultivates and accumulates all roots of goodness.
One is never satiated with meditative concentration because it is associated with its objects;
one is never satiated with wisdom because it involves skillful discernment in all circumstances for the sake of the benefit of the Dharma.
Wealth, happiness, and longevity are entirely without fault in every respect;
furthermore, one who practices correctly should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
As stated in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "O youth!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should fulfill one dharma; if they accomplish this merit, they will swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
What is this one dharma? Young man!

It is that a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of equanimity, a mind of benefit, a mind free from obstruction, and a mind free from malice; this is the one dharma.
Those who wish to practice the True Dharma should abandon matters such as gain and honor.
As stated in the *Cittaviveka-sūtra*: "One should examine all matters of gain, for attachment to them causes the loss of right mindfulness;
when delusion arises, it accomplishes one's own self-interest."
When flattery arises, one is unable to comply with the instructions and exhortations of all Buddhas;
when arrogance and conceit arise, they serve exclusively as the root of all that is treacherous and evil.
Because these things destroy and ruin all roots of goodness, the wise should carefully examine gain and honor.

Although one may obtain something in the present life, there will be no benefit or fruit whatsoever in future lives; one will be utterly estranged from immeasurable meditative concentrations and shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Furthermore, the wise person should investigate gain and offerings as being like the continuous flow of water.
Having investigated them in this way, they should give rise to a mind of few desires and contentment.
As it is said in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*: "For example, it is like a flock of mute sheep that circles around a nyagrodha tree."

Among them was one mute sheep that went alone to the place where the deer-keeper was at the Deer Rock; it even went before the herd of deer, wagging its head and kneeling down, seeking both their food and protection.
When he had returned in this manner, the rest of the flock of mute sheep all treated him with contempt.

Likewise, there is a class of monks who praise gain and harbor pride; they give rise to insatiable desires and depart from the community. For the sake of food, they enter cities and towns alone, wandering about to beg for alms and seeking invitations, thereby obtaining the most excellent and pure food and drink.
Having finished his own meal, he took the food he had requested back to where the assembly of bhikṣus was in the monastery and said to them:
"Venerable sirs!
Today, at the house of a layperson, I accepted their invitation and obtained that most excellent, pure food."
"Now I have this food which was begged for; it is food that has been prepared for long-term storage and is already relinquished. Venerable sirs, if you wish to eat, you may do so as you please."
When these words were spoken, the young bhikṣus among them all gave rise to contempt.
The wise should know that those who utter such coarse and evil speech do so for the sake of gain and other such matters, as explained at length in the sūtras.
In this context, how does one distance oneself from the two factors of guile (*śāṭhya*) and deceit (*māyā*)?
As stated in the *Anavatapta-gāthā*: "There are two factors that act as obstacles to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*): namely, first, deceit; second, guile."
There are two qualities that are unobstructed: first, uprightness; second, freedom from guile.
If one wishes to accomplish all correct practices, one should always draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), for it is through spiritual friends that all correct practices are accomplished.
In which sūtra is this stated? As it says in the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-siṃhavijṛmbhita-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

"Because of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), all the dharmas of the bodhisattva practices flow forth from the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Spiritual friends possess great majestic power and are able to bring all bodhisattvas to full accomplishment; spiritual friends are able to give birth to all the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of all bodhisattvas."
A spiritual friend is one who can universally compile and collect all the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas.
A spiritual friend serves as the root, for they are able to cause the profound resolve of all Bodhisattvas to be pure.
A spiritual friend is one who can provide protection and cause all accumulations of merit to increase;
a spiritual friend is that which is cherished for the attainment of the bodhi of all Buddhas.

A spiritual friend is able to sustain and uphold one, ensuring that all bodhisattvas do not fall into the evil destinies, causing them not to regress from the Great Vehicle and not to transgress the bodhisattva precepts; they lead them beyond the stage of foolish ordinary beings, yet do not abandon the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, while further acting as their protector.

A spiritual friend is one who can cause all those who have lost their way to return to the right path, and who, upon hearing the true Dharma, leads them to understand and enter into all Buddha-dharmas.
Spiritual friends are like mothers, for they enable all beings to be born into the family of the Buddhas.
Spiritual friends are like fathers, for they extensively provide for, nurture, and benefit sentient beings.
A spiritual friend is like a wet nurse, for they skillfully protect all beings so that they may remain free from sinful karma.
A spiritual friend is like a servant who endures toil, for they are able to enter the great ocean of afflictions within birth and death in order to rescue and deliver others.
A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is like a helmsman, for they transport sentient beings to the great jewel island of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Those who practice correctly and wish to go to the presence of a spiritual friend should form this mental resolve: they should make their body and mind pure and diligent; their mind should be like the earth, for it can bear all heavy burdens;
their mind should be like a servant, performing whatever instructions are given to them.
One's mind is like a dog, for it is constantly alert and barking to serve as a guard and protector.
One should regard oneself as a patient, the spiritual friend as a physician, the Dharma taught as medicine, and the practice according to those instructions as the healing of the illness.

In all such cases, once one has attained purity of the profound mind through spiritual friends, one practices well according to the teachings and instructions of those spiritual friends, thereby able to increase all roots of goodness.
Just as all medicinal herbs and forest groves rely upon the King of Snowy Mountains, so too does one who relies upon a spiritual friend become a great vessel for accomplishing all the Buddha-dharmas.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean is the destination to which all streams flow, because the bodhisattva is born from that [ocean] by means of spiritual friends, they immediately achieve the perfect fulfillment of all bodhisattva practices and all Buddha-dharmas.
As stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the Buddha said: "Kāśyapa,
it is like a person who boards a boat and enters the great ocean, but while in mid-stream, the boat suddenly breaks apart."
In this regard, some may rely upon a single plank of wood or other rafters; depending on what they find to rely upon, they reach the shore in safety.

Kāśyapa, it is just so with the Bodhisattva who boards the ship of the mind of omniscience: even if that ship of the Bodhisattva vehicle should suddenly break apart and be lost in midstream, if he encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and takes them as his support, he will immediately recover the mind of omniscience and, riding upon the dharmas of the various pāramitās, he shall carry himself across and reach the continent of the Dharma-realm.
Kāśyapa! All dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi depend entirely upon spiritual friends; therefore, making offerings to and serving spiritual friends is the most supreme practice.

Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, one should practice with diligence; thus one shall attain immeasurable merit and the perfection of practice, and ultimately bring all karmic fruits to full realization.
As stated in the *Kusuma-avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "If one sees the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita and, having seen him, gives rise to a pure mind and makes offerings;
or if, after that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, one takes even as much as a mustard seed of his relics and makes offerings to them."
The karmic fruits thus obtained are entirely equal, and therein there is no distinction of any kind.
As stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Ānanda!..."
Setting aside for a moment the case of one who makes offerings to me while I am present,
suppose there is another person who, after my parinirvāṇa, collects even as much as a mustard seed’s worth of my relics and performs various offerings to them.
"Setting aside this matter, suppose there is someone who constructs a jeweled stupa within my Dharma.

Setting that aside as well, if there should be someone who merely scatters a single flower into the air while visualizing the Buddhas as an act of offering—I declare that by virtue of these roots of goodness, such a person will ultimately attain the fruit of Great Nirvana."

Ānanda! To speak briefly, even for those sentient beings down to those in the animal realm, if they can bring the Buddhas to mind, I declare that by means of this root of goodness, they will ultimately attain the fruit of great parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda! Observe within the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One: what kind of giving constitutes the greatest?
What kind of resolve possesses such great power?
Ānanda! If there is anyone who can even once utter "Namo Buddhāya," this is the supreme meaning. Why is that?
This refers to the fact that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses a great and non-empty reputation.
This meaning of "non-empty" is precisely what is expressed by "Namo Buddhāya.

Because no matter how slight a root of goodness one may have toward the Tathāgatas—down to even a single instance of generating a pure mind—none of these will ever be lost or destroyed; they will all lead ultimately to the realization of Nirvāṇa.
Ānanda! It is like a fisherman who, wishing to catch fish in a large pond, places a hook with bait into the water; the fish then vie with one another to swim about and eat it.
At that time, the fisherman, knowing the location of the fish, firmly secured his hook, rod, reel, and line, and slowly lowered the deep hook.
Once he had caught the fish, he placed it on dry land and took it as he desired for his use.

It is the same for a certain class of sentient beings in this world: having first generated a pure mind in the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and planted roots of goodness—even if it was merely a single instance of pure faith—those beings later commit evil deeds and, shrouded by karmic obstructions, are born in difficult circumstances. Subsequently, they again encounter the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who uses the wisdom of bodhi and the hook-line of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to pull those beings out from the stream of birth and death and place them on the shore of *nirvāṇa*.
The *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"O Lord of Nāgas!
If Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can fully possess eight dharmas, they will never be separated from the Buddhas."

What are these eight? First, instructing others to contemplate the image of the Buddha; second, serving the Tathāgata; third, constantly praising the Tathāgata; fourth, fashioning images of the Buddha; fifth, instructing others to contemplate the physical marks and signs of the Buddha; sixth, upon hearing the name of any Buddha in any buddha-field, immediately generating a supreme aspiration for that buddha-field; seventh, not giving rise to inferior thoughts; and eighth, giving rise to a vast mind to seek the wisdom of a Buddha.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, those who are able to adorn and purify the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata shall attain four kinds of supreme vows of purity.

What are the four? First, the pure vow to attain the most supreme physical marks; second, the pure vow to be fully endowed with the most supreme characteristics; third, the pure vow to cultivate and accumulate the most supreme steadfastness; and fourth, the pure vow to behold the Tathāgata in the most supreme manner.

That sutra further states: "If a person scatters flowers and applies fragrant ointments as an offering at the stupas and temples of the Tathāgata, that person shall obtain eight kinds of indestructible qualities."

What are the eight? First, the non-destruction of physical form; second, the non-destruction of wealth and happiness; third, the non-destruction of retinue; fourth, the non-destruction of pure precepts; fifth, the non-destruction of extensive learning; sixth, the non-destruction of tranquil concentration; seventh, the non-destruction of wisdom; and eighth, the non-destruction of vows.

If there are those who wish to create an image of the Tathāgata, they should do so according to their inclination, whether using earth, wood, iron, stone, ivory, or gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, coral, agate, and various shells or exquisite fragrances; or by creating a painting, or by making images on wooden boards or walls; or by cutting and inlaying them upon paper, silk, or brocade; or by making them anew, or by repairing and restoring old or damaged images of the Tathāgata.

Having acted thus, in the future one will not be born into a lowly family, nor into a family of evil karma, nor into a family of wrong views; the limbs of the body one receives shall be free from any deficiency.

Suppose there is one who has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution; if such a person can give rise to pure faith toward the Tathāgata and fashion an image of the Tathāgata, all their future karmic retributions for hell will be transformed from heavy to light, and they shall attain liberation through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles or other vehicles.

It is like a person whose body has been defiled by impurities, yet who is able to bathe it thoroughly and adorn it with exquisite perfumes; consequently, those foul and evil odors are dispersed without remainder.
It is likewise for those who have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution; by creating an image of the Buddha, their karmic offenses are extinguished without remainder.

Furthermore, even for one who has fully practiced the ten unwholesome actions, if they develop pure faith toward the Tathāgata, their karmic offenses will also be entirely extinguished. This principle is like throwing clarified butter into a fire, where it is completely consumed by the flames until not a trace remains; how much more so for one who possesses the supreme bodhicitta, or one who has gone forth from the household life and maintains pure precepts?
