Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Dharma Protector (Dharmarakṣa), a Śramaṇa of the Purple Robe and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma (Chuanfan Dashi), Vice Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Shaqing), and others. As stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "Suppose all sentient beings throughout the three realms were each to construct stūpas and temples for the Tathāgata; and suppose these structures, in their form and appearance, were each as lofty and prominent as Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and that these sentient beings were to honor and make offerings to these stūpas for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."

If there is a bodhisattva who does not depart from the mind of omniscience and offers even a single flower as an act of worship, the mass of merit they obtain will be many times greater than the previous mass of merit.

That sutra further states: "Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to dwell entirely in the Mahāyāna and each became a universal monarch (cakravartin). Even if they were to take fragrant oil as vast as the waters of the great ocean and stack incense-wick grass equal in volume to Mount Sumeru, and each were to light such a vast lamp and offer it to all the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata."

If there is a renunciant bodhisattva who takes *dīpavartī* grass and, having applied a small amount of oil, offers it as a lamp before a Buddha stūpa, the mass of merit obtained from this is many times superior to the previous gift of lamps; the former does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor even one *upaniṣad*-part.
Furthermore, if those various Universal Monarchs were each to universally bestow all articles of enjoyment and comfort upon the Buddhas and the assembly of bhikṣus,

and there were a renunciant bodhisattva who, from the food begged with his own bowl, first reduced his portion to give to others before eating himself, the mass of merit obtained by this latter would surpass the former mass of merit, being most supreme and vast.
Furthermore, if those various Wheel-Turning Kings were to accumulate exquisite robes equal in volume to Mount Sumeru and bestow them universally upon the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus;

and if there were a renunciant bodhisattva who, with only the three robes, were to give them either to a bodhisattva of the ten levels of faith, or to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, or to a stūpa or temple of the Tathāgata—the accumulation of merit obtained by this latter would be far more excellent than that of the former gift.
Furthermore, if those various Wheel-Turning Kings were each to cover the entirety of Jambudvīpa with exquisite flowers as an extensive offering to the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata;

If there is a renunciant bodhisattva who, at the very least, takes up even a single flower to make an offering to a stūpa or temple of the Tathāgata, the mass of merit obtained by this person cannot be matched by the previous gift, even by a hundredth part, nor even by an *upaniṣad* part.

The *Anupūrvasamudgata-sūtra* states: "One should contemplate that there are four kinds of noble and praiseworthy qualities in a bodhisattva, for which one should exert oneself in making offerings to the Tathāgata."
What are the four? First, one personally performs the supreme practice of giving and making offerings, and causes other sentient beings to likewise perform such superior acts of offering;
second, having diligently and sincerely made offerings to all Tathāgatas, one further strengthens the great bodhicitta.
Third, one clearly perceives the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
fourth, one plants roots of goodness that become increasingly superior.
These four dharmas constitute the supreme service and offering to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Sāgaramati!
There are three supreme methods for serving and making offerings to the Tathāgata."
What are these three?

First, the generation of the great bodhicitta; second, the upholding of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma; and third, the extensive arousal of great compassion for sentient beings. These constitute the practice of ultimate worship.
The *Maitreya-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "There is no Buddha to be conceptualized and no Buddha to be perceived; how much less could there be a Buddha to be made offerings to?
For one who holds to the notion of attainment, such a thing is impossible."
Among these, what constitutes making an offering to the Buddha?
That which is called true offering should involve giving rise to a mind that is without conceptualization and without signs.

If there is no mental activity of the mind, no perception of a Buddha, no perception of Dharma, no perception of the Saṅgha, no perception of a person (pudgala), and no perception of self or other—such an offering is the true offering to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"O Lord of Devas!

Suppose worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with the relics of the Tathāgata and placed atop victory banners; if someone were to write out this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and offer both as gifts, which of these two portions would you choose?"
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Of these two portions, I shall take the portion of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? Because Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to the Tathāgata’s śarīra.
If there are those who make offerings to and cultivate Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby making offerings to the Tathāgata’s śarīra.
The Buddha said:
"Śakra! If there are sentient beings who have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s true nirvāṇa, they are extremely rare to find."
Among these, what is the true nirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas?
It is so stated in countless sūtras.
The *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-sūtra* records the Buddha saying:
O Son of the Buddha!

If bodhisattvas desire to fully understand the great parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, they should first, through the observation of wisdom, understand the nature of the self-nature of phenomena.

The intrinsic nature of phenomena refers to suchness, the limit of reality, the dharma-realm, the realm of space, the limit of natural purity, the limit of signlessness, the limit of the self-nature of the self, and the suchness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, which is nirvana.
One should understand the Tathāgata’s true parinirvāṇa in this way.
Why is that? O Son of the Buddha!
All phenomena are from the very beginning thus: without arising and without that which arises.
Since phenomena are from the very beginning thus—without arising and without that which arises—therefore not even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended.

However, when a Buddha-Tathāgata appears to be born, it is solely for the sake of causing the continuity of joy and happiness among sentient beings; likewise, when a Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, it is also for the sake of causing sentient beings to weary of birth. In reality, the Tathāgata is fundamentally neither born nor does he enter nirvāṇa.
These Tathāgatas eternally abide in the dharma-realm.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the appearance of the sun’s radiance, which universally illumines all worlds; within each pure vessel of water, the reflection of the sun is seen, yet it is not that the solar orb itself pervades all places—it appears only as it enters into the vessels.
Furthermore, whenever those various vessels of pure water are broken, become turbid, or diminish, the light of the sun is no longer seen at all.
However, although the reflection of the sun’s light does not appear within the vessel, this is not the fault of the sun, for it is due to the vessel itself being impaired.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata is also like this.
The sun-disk of the Dharma-realm, with its vast and great radiance, constantly emerges from within the Dharma-realm, universally illuminating and conforming to all worlds.
If sentient beings possess a continuum of pure minds, the Tathāgata manifests as a reflected image for them.
Although all sentient beings constantly behold the reflected image of the Tathāgata’s solar orb, it is not that the Tathāgata appears everywhere in accordance with their needs.

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who are like those broken vessels—because their mental continuums are impure and covered by karma and afflictions—they do not see the reflection of the Tathāgata’s sun-like radiance; those sentient beings then conceive the notion that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
However, as for the Tathāgata entering nirvāṇa, it is not the fault of the Tathāgata; it is only because the continuity of the roots of goodness of sentient beings is subject to destruction.

Furthermore, because there are sentient beings who must be transformed and delivered by means of the Dharma of Great Nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata manifests entry into nirvāṇa; yet in reality, the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes, nor does he abide anywhere.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like this: for example, when all the worlds are engaged in the business of fire, or later at some time, the fires in certain distinct villages, countries, cities, and towns are extinguished; yet it is not the case that the fires throughout the entirety of all worlds have been extinguished.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata is likewise: throughout all worlds, he universally performs all buddha-activities in accordance with circumstances.
Even if in other buddha-fields he has performed his buddha-activities and manifests entry into nirvāṇa, it is not the case that the Buddhas of all worlds have all entered nirvāṇa.

Just as a skilled illusionist who has well studied the arts of illusion and thoroughly mastered the power of all secret mantras manifests his body throughout all the trichiliocosms to perform various illusory feats, displaying them everywhere in all villages, lands, cities, and towns.

According to the power of his illusion, whether he remains for an eon or more than an eon, or within other villages or cities, once he has performed illusory acts, he conceals his own physical form; yet it is not the case that all illusory phenomena in the world are thereby concealed.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata is likewise; by means of immeasurable, illusion-like wisdom, having skillfully mastered the light of knowledge through the superior wisdom of expedient means, he manifests all illusory phenomena within the entire dharma-realm.

The Tathāgata appears in accordance with [the needs of beings], yet the body of the Tathāgata ultimately abides within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*). Having performed various deeds for the equal benefit of all sentient beings across diverse buddha-fields, he manifests *nirvāṇa*; however, it is not that he enters *nirvāṇa* within only a single buddha-field, for thus all Tathāgatas throughout the entire realm of phenomena enter *nirvāṇa*.

O Son of the Buddha! All Bodhisattvas should understand it thus: because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have attained Great Parinirvāṇa, that which they know is immeasurable and ultimately unattached; the Dharma-realm is boundless and likewise has no center. Its self-nature is as vast as the realm of empty space; True Suchness is unborn and yet unceasing, abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet manifesting through skillful means according to the occasion.

Therefore, you should know that you must not give rise to weariness or fatigue regarding all worlds; rather, abide securely according to your prior vows and accomplish all sublime dharmic practices throughout all worlds and all buddha-fields.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that great nirvāṇa is what is called emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
If one can awaken to and realize the nature of equality of all those phenomena, that is Great Nirvāṇa.
That sutra further states: The Buddha said, "Good son!..."

The Tathāgata has completed all that was to be done; since his attainment of Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed, and his lifespan is immeasurable. The Tathāgata abides eternally and does not enter nirvāṇa, yet for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests the appearance of nirvāṇa.
Why is this? It is because one should bring sentient beings to maturity through such conditions.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
Mahābrahmā!

Thus, when the karma of this world is exhausted, the afflictions are exhausted, and suffering is exhausted; when the conditions for suffering are extinguished and one attains tranquil transcendence—this is called nirvāṇa.
"Mahābrahmā!
Within this, there is no further person who realizes this nirvāṇa; it is the exhaustion of karma and afflictions, which is intrinsically pure.
As the "Chapter on Transcending the World" states: "The Buddhas, through their skillful means, reveal and demonstrate the boundless dharma of nirvāṇa."
The *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!
If those who have left the household life can bring to rest all phenomena according to their inclinations, this is called nirvāṇa."
The Buddha said:
"Mahābrahmā! This is because they are established through mutual conditionality."
The *Vipula-jñāna-sūtra* states that the Buddha said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
In the past there was a buddha named Uccagāmin; in his buddha-field, there were exclusively a community of śrāvakas."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Samatā who, observing all objects of perception, dwelt in the practice of the Mahāyāna.

This person had planted roots of goodness under immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of buddhas; his mind for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi had never regressed, and he dwelt securely within the unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma, desiring to purify unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.

In that buddha-field, there are no other sentient beings who have resolved to attain bodhicitta; at that time, although that bhikṣu has extensively planted roots of virtue, he gives rise to a mind of contempt toward the profound Dharma. For this reason, he shall be reborn in the long-lived heavens.

Then, after the Tathāgata Renowned and Lofty Fame had performed the Buddha-activities as was appropriate, he immediately surveyed all Buddha-fields: "In which fields do sentient beings not perform the Buddha-activities?"
Upon returning, he observed within his own buddha-field that there was a bhikṣu who dwelt in the practice of the Mahāyāna and was a vessel for bodhi.
However, that bhikṣu encountered obstacles because he had been reborn in the long-lived heavens; consequently, his physical vessel was incapable of being made to plant the roots of merit for bodhi.
After this person’s life ends, they shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell; furthermore, they will be incapable of planting the roots of merit for Bodhi.

Once they have emerged from hell and are born among humans, they will be deaf and mute; whatever they do, they will point with their hands to indicate things, or require the mediation of others before they can understand a matter.

At that time, the Tathāgata Yaśaḥpraghoṣa, desiring to transform and deliver that bhikṣu, employed skillful means; throughout sixty koṭi-nayuta births, he endured toil and suffering to perform various acts of transformation so as to bring him to maturity.
The Buddha said:

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! Behold how that Tathāgata, out of his great compassionate heart, endured such toil and hardship for the sake of a single sentient being over such a long period of time, until that bhikṣu’s conditions ripened and he came to abide in the stage of non-retrogression."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana! What do you think?
Was that Tathāgata named Yaśas-kīrti-prakāśa anyone other than this person?
He was none other than the Tathāgata Sarvārthasiddha.
As for those bhikṣus who contemplated all objects of focus, they were none other than the Tathāgata Amitābha.
The *Pitāputrasamāgamana-sūtra*, in the chapter on "Previous Conduct," states that the Buddha said:

Mañjuśrī! In that past cycle of saṃsāra, immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, and beginningless eons ago, there was a Tathāgata named Indradhvaja. He traversed as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and within all those buddha-fields, every sentient being attained five kinds of happiness: some attained the happiness of sensual desires, some attained the happiness of renunciation, some attained the happiness of dhyāna-concentration, some attained the happiness of samādhi, and some attained the happiness of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Although those sentient beings experience various pleasures, they are without attachment, just as a bird soaring through the air moves with complete mastery.
The experience of pleasure by those sentient beings is likewise entirely free from clinging.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That Tathāgata Indradhvaja at that time was none other than our World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha."
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states in verse:
"I do not perceive tranquility, Nor do I give rise to mental formations;
Furthermore, being free from discursive thought, I have thus realized nirvāṇa."
In this regard, it should be understood that faith and understanding in the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) are extremely difficult to find.
As for this One Vehicle, it is taught in all the sūtras. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"I have set forth the One Vehicle to teach the Dharma to sentient beings; that is to say, the Buddha-vehicle, which is neither two nor three."
In all worlds of the ten directions, it is the natural law that such is the case. Why is this?
Because in all the worlds of the ten directions throughout the past, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have likewise set forth the Single Vehicle to teach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
If, in future ages, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas in all worlds throughout the ten directions likewise give rise to the One Vehicle and preach the Dharma for sentient beings;

and if, in the present, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas in all worlds throughout the ten directions likewise give rise to the One Vehicle and preach the Dharma for sentient beings—namely, the Buddha Vehicle.
For this reason, even in the worlds of the ten directions there is not even the establishment of the two vehicles, let alone the three.
The "Chapter on Reality" states that the Buddha said: "O Mañjuśrī!"

Because the realm of the One Vehicle was fully perfected during his former causal stage, in this present Buddha-field there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle as the means of transcendence, and no establishment of the two vehicles of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already abandoned all manifold conceptualizations.
If someone were to say:
Whether the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, or the Pratyekabuddhayāna, or the Śrāvakayāna,
such a person gives rise toward the Tathāgata to an impure mind, an unequal mind, and a mind of grasping attachment.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"If I were to speak of various conceptualizations, I would be generating deceit and crookedness within the Dharma myself.

However, all the dharmas I teach for the sake of sentient beings are entirely intended to cause them to aspire to bodhi, to embrace the Mahāyāna, and to attain omniscience; thus, I lead all sentient beings together to the ground of the knowledge of all modes of knowing (*sarvajñajñāna*)."

Therefore, there are no stages of those various vehicles to be established, nor are there any stages established by me; nor do I establish the status of a *pudgala*, nor is there anything established by means of either limited practice or immeasurable practice; furthermore, there are no three vehicles to be differentiated.

That non-conceptual nature is the gateway to the Dharma-realm; it is taught through skillful means for the sake of conventional truth alone to provide guidance and instruction, yet within ultimate truth, there is only the Single Vehicle and no duality.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"O Lord of Devas!
If there are among the sons of gods those who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall cause them to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Furthermore, if there are those who are unable to resolve upon the aspiration for bodhicitta, I shall also cause them to rejoice in the generation of the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Why is this? Because their continuity remains uninterrupted within the flow of birth and death.
It is not my intention that any portion of those roots of goodness should be obscured; rather, I shall cause them to attain realization within the most supreme Dharma.
The "Chapter on the Great Assembly" states: "The One Vehicle universally encompasses all vehicles, because the One Vehicle subsumes all vehicles.
They equally return to the single principle and universally enter the non-discriminatory nature of the Dharma-realm."
The *Dhāraṇīśvararāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The Buddha does not speak of various conceptualizations.
Nevertheless, when the Buddha appears in the world, all his activities are of a single flavor within the dharmadhātu, and he remains unobstructed in his capacity to embrace all sentient beings."

Having attained perfect enlightenment for oneself, one further causes all sentient beings to likewise awaken; thereafter, one turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma, namely, the wheel of non-retrogression.

It is like a master gem-cutter who, at a place where jewels are found, takes only a piece of artificial-colored glass; he first polishes it with alkaline water to make it clean, and subsequently treats it further with black, oily hair.

Yet the master jeweler never grew weary; subsequently, he polished and refined it further with meat broth and fine silk, and then processed it sequentially with the juice of great medicinal herbs and exquisite fabrics until it became lustrous and pure, its artificial color removed so that it was identical to genuine lapis lazuli.

The Tathāgata is likewise in this regard: knowing that the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally impure, he proclaims the teachings of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, causing them to conceive a sense of weary detachment toward saṃsāra. Thereafter, through the skillful means of taming with the noble Dharma, he guides them; yet the Tathāgata does not for a moment give rise to weariness.
Subsequently, he proclaims the teachings of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, causing them to open the eye of the Tathāgata; yet the Tathāgata does not for a moment give rise to weariness.

Finally, he proclaims the wheel of non-retrogression and the purity of the three wheels, leading sentient beings to enter the realm of the Tathāgata, where they equally transcend all causal natures and fully realize the pure *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata.
This is called attaining the ultimate, unsurpassed fruit within the world.
The *Avaivartika-sūtra* states: "Because the wheel of non-retrogression is equal, the Dharma taught by all Buddhas is also equal."

Therefore, because sentient beings of inferior faith and understanding are unable to comprehend the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) Dharma, the Tathāgata has appeared within the five turbidities of this Sahā world; employing skillful means, he establishes buddha-works for those sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

The *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, skillfully proclaim this Dharma of Nirvāṇa, from which all vehicles arise within the context of the Three Vehicles; yet, it is by means of the Dharma of the One Vehicle that one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The seeds of all afflictions enter into *samādhi* and *samāpatti*; through realizing them as they truly are, one abides in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Furthermore, entering into the untainted realms of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, one brings to perfection the supramundane sublime practices and attains mastery over the inconceivable *dharmakāya*."
In order to bring about virtuous practices for the sake of sentient beings to be converted, the Tathāgatas employ skillful means to teach various vehicles.
Therefore, within the diverse realms of beings, the Tathāgatas do not merely teach the three vehicles, but also teach other methods of the Dharma.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: In the world-system of the Auspicious Liberation of Great Vairocana, the Tathāgata Universal Wisdom Flame Merit Banner King establishes immeasurable sentient beings in the stage of the śrāvaka and brings immeasurable sentient beings to maturity in the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha.
The birth of bodhi through the swift eloquence that matures immeasurable sentient beings;
the birth of bodhi through the stainless banner of diligence that matures immeasurable sentient beings;
the birth of bodhi through the dharma-eloquence that matures immeasurable sentient beings.
The arising of enlightenment through the maturation of immeasurable sentient beings, the purification of their faculties, and the production of eloquence;
the arising of enlightenment through the maturation of immeasurable sentient beings, the ten powers, and the fulfillment of all practices;
the arising of enlightenment through immeasurable sentient beings abiding in the city of Dharma and manifesting the realm of the One Vehicle.
Innumerable sentient beings give birth to bodhi by manifesting various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) in all places according to the principle of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Innumerable sentient beings give birth to bodhi by establishing all practices and universally encompassing immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*).
Innumerable sentient beings give birth to bodhi by abiding in the principle of the stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Immeasurable sentient beings dwell securely in the maṇḍala of the pure path of all objects of focus; immeasurable sentient beings give rise to bodhicitta through the principle of the emergence of awakening;
immeasurable sentient beings develop the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva;
and immeasurable sentient beings abide in the bodhisattva path.
Immeasurable sentient beings abide in the path of the pure pāramitās;
immeasurable sentient beings dwell in the first bodhisattva ground, up to and including dwelling in the tenth bodhisattva ground.
In this regard, it should be understood that a bodhisattva always gathers and sustains all beings through the true Dharma.
What is this gathering and sustaining through the true Dharma?
As stated in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī! Because the True Dharma is embraced, the Bodhisattva is embraced; because the Bodhisattva is embraced, the True Dharma is embraced.
Because the True Dharma is embraced, all sentient beings are embraced; because all sentient beings are embraced, the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed and their activities are accomplished.

Furthermore, if one wishes to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed; if one wishes to destroy all the karmic afflictions of sentient beings; if one wishes to close the gates to all evil destinies; if one wishes to experience the supreme and wondrous pleasures of immeasurable and innumerable universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), as well as the joys of Brahmā kings, Śakra, and the world-protectors; if one wishes to sever all the snares of Māra; and even if one wishes to attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one must in every case embrace them through the True Dharma.
In this regard, one should ask:
how does a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*) gather and uphold the True Dharma with such meager roots of virtue?

As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, if a bodhisattva possesses four qualities, they shall not diminish in their progress toward awakening; in their subsequent birth, they will become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). By the power of their vows, all roots of virtue will follow them in transformation, and they will attain a body as powerful and firm as that of Nārāyaṇa. Having become a universal monarch, they will cultivate the four brahma-vihāras and be reborn in the Brahma-world as the Lord of the Brahmas.
What are the four?

First, if a bodhisattva sees that a stūpa or temple of the Tathāgata has fallen into ruin, they arouse a mind of diligent vigor to restore and adorn it, even making an offering of it with a single lump of clay.

Second, at crossroads or in marketplaces, one may erect a lofty and magnificent stūpa for the Tathāgata, or a shrine with an image, or set up a banner or emblem, or simply plant a *yaṣṭi* (sacred pole), or install an image of the Tathāgata, or separately arrange various manifestations of the Tathāgata, namely: the manifestation of turning the wheel of Dharma; or the manifestation of leaving the city and renouncing the world; or the manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; or the manifestation of displaying great supernatural powers to subdue the armies of Māra; or the manifestation of entering Great Parinirvāṇa; or the manifestation of descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Third, if one sees those among the assembly of śrāvaka disciples who are divided, one shall bring them into harmony.

Fourth, within the teaching of the Tathāgata, if one sees that the True Dharma is about to decline and perish, one shall courageously protect and uphold it—even if only a single four-line verse—causing it to circulate so that it is not lost or forgotten.
Furthermore, one should embrace and uphold the True Dharma or the teacher who expounds it, never abandoning the Dharma even at the cost of sacrificing one’s own life.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"O son of noble family!..."
If a bodhisattva possesses ten qualities, they will be able to uphold the True Dharma. What are these ten?

First, during the final five hundred years of the latter age when the True Dharma declines, when confusion arises within the Tathāgata’s teaching, and when sentient beings mostly abide in false paths—the lamp of wisdom extinguished and no authentic teacher remaining—one should, at that time, respect, honor, uphold, recite, proclaim, and explain the vast sūtras; those which possess great power and encompass the vast meaning, serving as the mother of all dharmas.
Second, to expound, explain, and elucidate profound sutras for others so that they may understand them;
third, to give rise to a joyful and pure mind toward those who practice the correct path;
fourth, having attained such joy, to provide for their support and guidance.
Fifth, with a mind free from attachment, one teaches the Dharma to others so that they may hear and accept it;
sixth, one conceives the thought of the teacher toward those who preach the Dharma;
seventh, one conceives the thought of nectar toward the True Dharma.
Eighth, one should regard the true Dharma as excellent medicine;
ninth, one should seek the true Dharma without begrudging even body or life;
tenth, one should practice according to the teachings of the Dharma one has obtained.
These are the ten dharmas.
The *Śāntiniyatavikurvāṇa-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"Bhadrapāla!"
If a bodhisattva is endowed with four qualities, they are able to uphold the true Dharma.
What are these four? First, they do not crave or become attached to their own happiness.
Second, bestowing supreme and sublime happiness upon others;
third, possessing great compassion;
fourth, seeking the Dharma without weariness.

That sutra further states: In a past age, King Vimalatejas planted various roots of goodness for a thousand years in the presence of the Tathāgata Mahocchraya; he made offerings to that Buddha with every kind of article of pleasure and provided the four requisites to an assembly of eighty-four thousand bhikṣus.
After a thousand years had passed in this manner, that Tathāgata Mahocchuṣma addressed King Vimalatejaprabha, saying:

"Great King, if the roots of goodness produced by you while practicing various acts of giving in the presence of the Tathāgata for a full thousand years were compared to the roots of goodness contained within a single inhalation and exhalation of a Bodhisattva who diligently practices the quest for the Dharma, they would not equal even one hundredth part; indeed, they would not equal even an *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) fraction."
How much more so for one who diligently proclaims and explains the meaning of even a single four-line verse within the True Dharma—the limit of that merit I am unable to describe.
"Great King!
Let this matter rest for now.

Even if one were to fulfill a full thousand years in this manner, giving all that one possesses as offerings and gifts, and collecting them all together to bestow them upon a single wandering bhikṣu, or likewise bestowing them upon the entire assembly of bhikṣus."

If, toward those who diligently practice, proclaim, and expound the Bodhisattva teachings, one honors them out of a love for the Dharma, gives rise to pure faith, and offers food and drink while forming this thought:
"For the sake of seeking the true Dharma, I offer these foods and drinks as a gift."

If one were to compare the merit of former acts of giving with these roots of goodness, the former would not equal even a hundredth part of the latter; indeed, it would not even equal a fraction of an *upaniṣad*.
The *Tathāgata-rahasya-sūtra* states: "If one were to compare the mass of merit of all bodhisattvas with the mass of merit from upholding the true Dharma, the latter would be many times greater."
Even if all the Buddhas were to diligently proclaim it for ten million *koṭi* eons, they still could not reach the limit of the mass of merit from upholding the True Dharma.
What is this True Dharma?
As stated in the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, this True Dharma is a synonym for the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
Because the Mahāyāna gives birth to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.

The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* states: "That which upholds the True Dharma refers to the proclamation, instruction, and focused contemplation of all the extremely profound and most profound sūtras spoken by all Tathāgatas; this is what constitutes the upholding of the True Dharma."

It should be known that if bodhisattvas rely on practices based on grasping at attainments, even if they make offerings to all Tathāgatas for immeasurable time, they will not receive a prediction of enlightenment in the presence of those various Buddhas, much less achieve awakening.
As stated in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"O Great Brahmā!
Were I to spend an eon, or even more than an eon, I could proclaim the names of those various Tathāgatas."

Even though I have made offerings to these Tathāgatas, or have practiced the holy life and the six pāramitās under them, I have not yet received a prophecy of enlightenment from those various Buddhas.
Why is this? It is because I was attached to practices that involve the apprehension of something.

Had I, at that time in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, attained the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) as soon as I saw that Buddha, the World-Honored One would have conferred the prophecy upon me.

At that time, I transcended all practices involving objective apprehension and further perfected the six pāramitās; I was able to give rise to faith and understanding regarding the profound Dharma, and I brought to complete fulfillment all the supreme practices of bodhisattvas for their own benefit and the benefit of others.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, "Candragarbha-parivarta," states: The Buddha said, "Candragarbha!

That ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely that which can accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) cannot accomplish the supreme roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* nor bring about the various sublime practices."
Candragarbha!
It is like a person holding a torch who cannot dry up the profound great ocean.
The conventional truth is just like this: it cannot even dry up one's own ocean of afflictions, much less do so for other sentient beings.
In this regard, who is able to believe in and understand the profound Dharma?

As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, a bodhisattva possesses two kinds of wisdom: first, that which arises from the voices of others; second, that which arises from deep and firm mental attention within one's own mind.
Among these, who is the śrāvaka dependent on others?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, although he delights in practicing various forms of meditative application, does not delight in hearing or receiving the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, nor does he delight in hearing the noble Vinaya and Dharma. Because he finds satisfaction in the slight flavor of meditative concentration and his pride is intensely burning, he falls into overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Yet that bodhisattva is unable to liberate himself from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; nor is he able to liberate himself from the saṃsāra of the six destinies, and furthermore, he cannot liberate himself from the aggregate of suffering.
For that reason, the Tathāgata has said that one hears from others;
yet what is heard in this way cannot bring liberation from such phenomena as old age and death.
What, then, is profound and firm attention?

What is called the Bodhisattva’s own training is this: that there is no dharma whatsoever which can be joined together or not joined together; this is profound and firm practice. This profound and firm practice is a synonym for non-practice.
One thus examines that sound as it truly is, whether in the past or in the future: from what does it arise, and into what does it cease?

Furthermore, one examines as they truly are all things—whether speech or meaning, abandonment or realization, what has been said or what is yet to be said—and finds that none of them possess the characteristics of the past, the characteristics of the future, or the characteristics of the present; thus, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent.

The intrinsic nature is quiescent and intrinsically perfect; ultimately, all phenomena are without birth, without arising, and without reality. One should contemplate that all phenomena are ultimately in *nirvāṇa*.
If one contemplates in this way, there is neither an object of contemplation nor a lack of contemplation; this is called right contemplation.
How much less can all phenomena be observed as they truly are?
This is precisely that which is without an object of observation; this absence of an object of observation is itself a synonym for non-arising.
If all phenomena are non-arising, they do not transcend correct principle; if all phenomena are equal, the Buddha-dharma is equal.

What has been thus explained does not deviate from correct principle; this exposition is called "profound and firm mental attention," and in this way one is able to understand and enter the most supreme and profound True Dharma.
The *Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!
Suppose that during the period of the empty kalpa, a celestial palace of Brahmā were to appear before you, composed of the seven precious jewels and possessing a solid nature."
When they arise, from where do they come?

Thus, the celestial palaces of the various heavens—the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, and Cāturmahārājika heavens of the desire realm—all appear to be composed entirely of the seven precious jewels.
Furthermore, as for Mount Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa, which are composed of a single mass of solid diamond—whence does the solidity of these various mountains originate?

Furthermore, Mount Sumeru, Mount Nimindhara, Mount Yugaṃdhara, Mount Īṣādhara, Mount Kāñcanaparvata, Mount Khadiraka, Mount Vinataka, Mount Aśvakarṇa, Mount Sudarśana, Mount Mahāsudarśana, Mount Udayagiri, Mount Gandhamādana, Mount Himavat, and all other Black Mountains appeared before him; indeed, everything throughout the entire trichiliocosm appeared.
Furthermore, Great King, that Sumeru, King of Mountains, rises eighty thousand yojanas above the earth; from where does its solid and substantial nature entirely manifest before us?
Great King!

If, after this world has been formed, the great earth is consumed by fire, submerged by great waters, or battered by great winds, its flames will extend across the sky and all smoke and embers will completely vanish, just as when ghee or oil is cast into a fire and burned, leaving neither smoke nor residue.
When that water flows away, nothing remains; it is like salt cast into water, which completely dissolves and leaves no residue.
When that wind blows and strikes, not even the slightest thing can be seen; when the Vairambha wind blows, how could any flying bird be seen?
This trichiliocosm is likewise; when it is consumed by fire, swept away by water, or shattered by wind, nothing remains to be seen.
Since that solid nature is thus destroyed and ceases to exist, where could it go?
This explains the external earth element;
the internal earth element is likewise,
and the same applies to all other elements, whether internal or external.
Therefore, when all phenomena arise, they come from nowhere;
when they cease, they likewise go nowhere.
Those things that have arisen are necessarily all empty.
Once arisen, they too are by their very nature empty.

The *Ajātaśatru-kaukṛtya-vinodana Sūtra* states: At that time, King Ajātaśatru, within his palace, provided a meal for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Having washed his hands and cleansed his vessels, he sat with solemn reverence before the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī to listen to and receive the True Dharma.
The King said:
"O Bodhisattva!"
"I pray that you will now dispel my remorse.
Mañjuśrī said: "Great King!"
"Even if there were as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they too would be unable to dispel your remorse.
Upon hearing these words, King Ajātaśatru was struck with such terror and despair that he fell to the ground, gasping for breath.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the king, saying:
"Stop, stop!
Great King!"
Do not give rise to fear or alarm.
This Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is well able to explain his own causes and conditions for you; you should ask him this question:
"For what reason does the Bodhisattva speak thus?"
Then King Ajātaśatru slowly rose from the ground and addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
saying, "For what reason does the Bodhisattva speak thus? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Great King!
What do you think? Does your mind have an object upon which it contemplates the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"
The King said, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"How do you now observe the arising of the mind?
The King replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "Does one contemplate the extinction of the mind?
The King replied:
"No. Mañjuśrī asked: "Do you observe conditioned phenomena?"
The King said: "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Do you observe that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has any indication regarding conditioned phenomena?
The King replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "Great King, what do you think?"
"If among all phenomena there is no phenomenon that can be observed,
could there possibly be a phenomenon that can be dispelled?
The King said:
"No. Mañjuśrī said, "Great King!"
For this reason, I say that even if there were as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they would not be able to dispel your remorse.
Furthermore, Great King!
Suppose there were smoke or dust in this space that sought to defile the void—what do you think?
Could that smoke or dust defile the void?
The King said, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Great King!
Furthermore, there may be someone who says:
'I wish to purify space.'"
"And would that space be able to become pure?
The King replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "Great King,
the Tathāgata is likewise equal to space."

It is taught that all phenomena are, from the very beginning, a continuous succession whose intrinsic nature is undefiled; since there is no phenomenon whatsoever—whether defiled or pure—that can be truly perceived, what further thing is there within this to be removed?
"Great King!
It is because I have contemplated this matter as it truly is that I speak thus:
even if there were as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they would likewise be unable to dispel your remorse."
Furthermore, Great King!
Within the minds of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there is nothing attained and nothing arisen; externally, likewise, there is nothing attained and nothing arisen.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is without arising.
Since the intrinsic nature of phenomena is without arising, there is no locus that can accommodate an arising nature.
Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) have no arising by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*), they are not established;
because all phenomena are not established, they do not accumulate; because all phenomena do not accumulate, they are not produced. All phenomena...
Because there is no arising, phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, there is no activity of an agent;
because all phenomena lack the activity of an agent, there is no birth;
because all phenomena have no birth, there is no dharma of maturation; because all phenomena have no maturation, there is no origination. One...
Because all phenomena are without arising or activity, they are without defilement; because all phenomena are without defilement, their intrinsic nature is luminous;
because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is luminous, phenomena are pure;
because all phenomena are pure, they are equal to space; because all phenomena are equal to space, they are without antidote. One...
Because all phenomena lack an antidote, they are free from duality; because all phenomena are free from duality, they are free from the two extremes;
because all phenomena are free from the two extremes, phenomena are boundless; because all phenomena are boundless, they are without limit;
because all phenomena are without limit, they have no ultimate end. All phenomena...
Because there is no ultimate, there is no object of cognition; because all phenomena lack an object of cognition, they abide without inversion in all places;
and because all phenomena abide without inversion in all places, permanence, bliss, self, and purity are entirely unobtainable.
Because all phenomena are eternal, they correspond to being without movement or transition;
because all phenomena are pure, they are constituted by the luminosity of their own nature; because all phenomena are blissful, they correspond to non-conceptuality;
because all phenomena have the self as their own nature, they correspond to the representation of non-self; because all phenomena are without regret...
The inner mind is stilled; because all phenomena lack substantial reality, they are not established within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because all phenomena are quiescent, they possess the characteristic of universal stillness. Because all phenomena are selfless, they are free from the characteristics of "self" and "mine.
Because all phenomena are flavorless, they possess the characteristic of liberation. All phenomena are devoid of names.
Therefore, because distinctions in names are unattainable, all phenomena are free from conceptual differentiation;
because all phenomena are of a single flavor, they universally encompass liberation; because all phenomena are devoid of characteristics, they are the limit of signlessness;
and because all phenomena are without signs, they are the purity of the non-apprehension of objects of cognition.
Because all phenomena are empty, one is detached from all views and mental constructions;
because all phenomena are wishless, one transcends the three periods of time; because all phenomena are severed from the three periods of time, the past, future, and present are all unattainable;
and because all phenomena are universally encompassed by nirvāṇa, they are ultimately without arising.
"Great King! What do you think?
If a phenomenon is without arising and without accumulation, could it still be subject to defilement therein?"
The King said: "No. Mañjuśrī said:
Furthermore, is there any dharma that can be dispelled?
The King replied: "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "Great King!
It is because of this that the Tathāgata knows all phenomena to be equal to nirvāṇa; thus, within this state, there is no remorse that can be dispelled."
Therefore, Great King!
One should practice that profound and firm correspondence in this way; with a mind free from inversion, one should conduct such investigation in accordance with reality.
When one has thus investigated and continues to investigate accordingly, there is not the slightest phenomenon to be grasped or rejected, nor is there any phenomenon with which one may coexist.
Because all phenomena do not coexist, this is called pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

If a phenomenon is pliancy, that phenomenon is tranquility; if a phenomenon is tranquility, it is the intrinsic nature of phenomena; if a phenomenon is intrinsic nature, it is the absence of intrinsic nature. Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are without a master.
"Great King!
Within this, you should practice the dharma of patience; yet even here, there is no dharma that can be practiced. Why is this?"
"Great King!
Because that which is done is quiescent, one who realizes this shall realize nirvāṇa; herein there is neither any dharma to be performed, nor is there non-performance."
Whether it be that which is created or that which is uncreated, all such teachings ultimately lead to the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
*Mahāyāna-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven;

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Dharma Master of Radiant Purity, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing, and others, by imperial decree:

At that time, King Ajātaśatru took a most excellent cotton garment (*karpāsa*) worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces] and offered it as a gift to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. However, the Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept it; the king then immediately draped this exquisite cotton garment over the body of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Before the robe had even touched his body, the Bodhisattva immediately vanished and became invisible.
Since the King could no longer see the Bodhisattva’s body, he heard a voice in the air saying:
"Great King!"
If you can see the physical form of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, you will be able to see all your misdeeds.
If you see your misdeeds, in that very way you will see all phenomena.
Just as one perceives all phenomena, so too should one perceive the cotton garment that has been offered.
If you are unable to see it, then see it in this manner.
Great King!
"If you can perceive the physical forms of these beings, then you may offer this cotton garment as a gift.

Thereupon, the king immediately took the cotton garments and distributed them one by one to the entire assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as to his palace women, maidservants, and retinue; yet he perceived no physical form whatsoever in any of them.

The king immediately entered meditative absorption and observed that there was not even the slightest form to be seen by the eye, nor any objective appearance to manifest; therein, only the mental impression of his own body persisted.
Furthermore, he heard such a voice in the air saying:
"If you can perceive the marks of your own body, then you may offer this cotton cloth as a gift.
The king immediately examined himself, yet he did not see any marks of his own body; at that moment, he was freed from all perceptions of form.
Again, a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"Great King!

The *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!
There are five dharmas for bodhisattvas that bring about peace and security, enabling them to purify the first bhūmi."
What are these five?

First, having personally established oneself in the wisdom of liberation that is without objective referents, one further causes others to likewise fully establish themselves in the wisdom of liberation that is without objective referents; this is the bodhisattva’s attainment of the dharma of peace and security.

Second, this liberation-wisdom that has no object of perception is the non-dual, the purity of non-duality, and the non-arising of conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*). Having established oneself in this liberation, one further causes others to likewise abide in the liberation of the non-arising of conditioned phenomena; this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the dharma of peace and security.

Third, because those conditioned phenomena are non-arising, the very nature of all conditions is non-arising; this is the sphere of non-existence of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Having established oneself securely within this liberation, one further causes others to likewise abide in this liberation of the sphere of non-existence of all phenomena. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to attain the dharma of peace and security.

Fourth, regarding the fact that all those phenomena have no locus of existence: the conceptual distinctions of all states are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; one contemplates them with wisdom as being like space. Having established oneself in this liberation, one further causes others to likewise abide in the dharma of the liberation of wisdom that is like space. This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the dharma of peace and security.

Fifth, this wisdom which is like space is a wisdom that is without confusion, without dependence, and free from mind, thought, and consciousness. Having established oneself in this liberation, one further causes others to likewise abide in the dharma of liberation—the wisdom free from mind, thought, and consciousness. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to attain the dharma of peace and security.
One should know that within this, the wisdom that is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness is precisely the wisdom of non-awakening and non-apprehension; these constitute the five dharmas.

Why is this? Because the Buddha’s wisdom is unattached, non-conceptual, ineffable, inexpressible, non-active, beyond the path of language, and transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness; whether it be a slight knowledge or universal knowledge, it is not easily understood.

Mañjuśrī said: "O Son of Heaven!
The Tathāgata, through skillful means, provisionally employs the wisdom of letters to awaken beings accordingly; yet this wisdom is itself devoid of letters."
It is like seeking fire within fire; what could possibly be obtained?
O Devaputra, the Tathāgata is also like this.
If one were to speak of the vast wisdom of the Buddha from the very beginning, no sentient being would be able to know that Buddha-wisdom.
Therefore, such words as these are spoken to reveal that wisdom; yet this wisdom is without letters.

If one speaks of the dharmas of maintaining ethical discipline and prohibitions, or speaks of dharmas associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or speaks of entering into and understanding the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma)—all such speech as this is merely conventional terminology."
"O Son of Heaven!

If one speaks of the Dharma that is free from arising and free from ceasing; free from speech concerning the mixed and the unmixed, and free from speech concerning defilement and purity; free from speech of wearying of or renouncing birth-and-death, and free from speech of rejoicing in or delighting in nirvāṇa; wherein there is no knowing, no abandoning, no cultivation, no realization, and no attainment, nor even any samādhi to be manifested—this is it."
What has been stated here constitutes pure and true speech, an inconceivable sound.
The *Sarvadharmanirvedhāpratilambha-sūtra* states that the Buddha asked Mañjuśrī:
"Regarding the inconceivable realm of the inconceivable spoken of by all Tathāgatas, how should it be understood?"
Mañjuśrī said: "World-Honored One, this inconceivable realm of the inconceivable is what all the Tathāgatas have taught."
The realm is free from discursive thought; it is not the domain of the mind, nor is it measurable by the mind, nor can it be discerned through mental phenomena.
World-Honored One, such is this mind, and it is precisely the inconceivable realm.
Why is this? Because there is no mind that can be contemplated; since this mind is free from contemplation, even the self-nature of the mind does not exist.
This non-contemplative mind is the mind as it truly is.
“World-Honored One!
This is indeed the inconceivable realm.
Furthermore, this sutra says that the Buddha spoke:
"Mañjuśrī! You should not don this armor to deliver sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Bhagavān! If one knows that the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases, how could there be any sentient being therein who could be transformed and led into nirvāṇa? Bhagavān!"
If there were someone capable of crossing over that space of emptiness, then those realms of sentient beings could likewise be transformed and delivered.

Furthermore, if one wishes to transform and deliver others by means of the bodhicitta, those sentient beings can likewise be inspired to do so for the sake of their own transformation and deliverance.
"Bhagavān! All phenomena are bodhi; yet neither bodhi nor the defilement or purity [of phenomena] can be apprehended. Therefore, Bhagavān, you have said:
'Do not don this armor to deliver sentient beings.'"
"Bhagavān! Sentient beings are not defiled, and I likewise do not abide in the mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings. Why is this?"
"Bhagavān! If there were sentient beings, then defilement and purity could be indicated;
since there are no sentient beings, how could defilement and purity be indicated?"
World-Honored One!
If dharmas exist, they arise from conditions; thus, there is no contradiction.
World-Honored One!

Within dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is in reality neither defilement nor purity to be found, because all phenomena lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and possess the nature of dependent origination.
Even within conditions (*pratyaya*), there is no meaning of conditions such that defilement or purity could be found.
"Bhagavān! This meaning of non-existence is the meaning of dependent origination, which the wise fully understand.

Furthermore, regarding this meaning of dependent origination, the wise have no conceptual discrimination whatsoever within it; and within this meaning of non-discrimination, there is neither defilement nor purity."
For example, suppose a magician or a magician’s apprentice conjures through illusion a multi-storied pavilion or a house, complete with vast and fiercely blazing flames.
Suppose someone were to say:

Such a person may even injure their own body, but they will only produce exhaustion in vain and ultimately fail to achieve it.
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"So it is, so it is. Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One!"
If one dons the armor of diligence to transform and deliver sentient beings in such a manner, one will merely exhaust oneself in vain and ultimately achieve nothing.
This sutra further states that the Buddha said: "O Mañjuśrī!"
"You should examine, in accordance with reality, what dharma this designation refers to. Mañjuśrī replied:
"This so-called 'examination in accordance with reality'—within such examination in accordance with reality, there is not even a single nature nor a manifold nature that can be produced."
"Bhagavān! If one performs a thorough investigation into that which is without category and without conceptual differentiation, it is not a thorough investigation as it truly is. Bhagavān!"
This "not investigating according to reality" is a metaphorical designation.
Therefore, once investigation has been accomplished in accordance with reality, the views that "I am an ordinary person" or "I am a noble one" do not arise therein.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have nothing upon which to rely.
If one does not establish the views of ordinary beings or noble ones regarding phenomena, then one attains the accomplishment of investigating according to reality.
“World-Honored One!

If a son or daughter of good family can abide in this manner, they will immediately attain correspondence with the dharma-realm; therein, not even the slightest dharma—whether of equality or of differentiation—is to be found.”
If one says that the various dharmas of ordinary beings do not give rise to discrimination,
or if one says that the equal dharmas of noble ones do not give rise to discrimination— why is this so?
Because the object of cognition (*ālambana*) cannot be apprehended.
If, within the object of cognition, there were anything grasped as either equal or distinct, that would be conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
This nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely non-existent.
If there were any equality or distinction to be grasped within those various objects of cognition, then "self-dharma" and "other-dharma" would indeed have a distinction.
In all such cases, one should know that, as a certainty, no dharma can be grasped.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "What is the root of illness?
It is said that having objects of attachment (*ālambana*) is the root of illness; if there is an object of attachment, there is illness."
What is it that serves as an object of attachment?
It is called the three realms.
If there were no object of attachment, what would it signify?
If that which is grasped as an object of perception cannot be apprehended, then there is nothing to be attained.
What is meant by "nothing to be attained"?
It means that the two views are not to be attained.
What are the two views?
They are the internal view and the external view.
In these, nothing is apprehended.
This sutra further states that the Bodhisattva Aijian said:

In this way, up to consciousness itself is emptiness; it is not that the cessation of consciousness constitutes emptiness, for the nature of consciousness is itself empty.
To understand these five aggregates in this manner is to enter the gate of non-dual dharma.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), how can they know skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)?"
Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not engage with form, nor do they engage with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not engage with the characteristic of form, nor even the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not engage with form as permanent or impermanent, suffering or happiness, self or non-self, still or moving, empty or non-empty, characterized or uncharacterized, wishful or wishless, detached or non-detached; and so on, up to not engaging with consciousness as permanent or impermanent, nor even as detached or non-detached, regarding the five aggregates."

In this way, all dhātus, āyatanas, dependently arisen phenomena, factors of enlightenment, supernormal powers, pāramitās, powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities, and so forth—even up to that which is neither separate nor not separate—are entirely non-active.
Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra!

Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. This extends even to consciousness, which is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from consciousness; consciousness is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself consciousness.

In this way, the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and even the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are not different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*); emptiness is not different from the unique qualities of a Buddha. The unique qualities of a Buddha are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the unique qualities of a Buddha.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner, they are thereby able to know skillful means (upāyakauśalya).

Furthermore, regarding that perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva does not think, "I am practicing," nor do they think, "I am not practicing," nor do they think, "I am both practicing and not practicing," nor do they think, "I am neither practicing nor not practicing."
Why is this? Because the self-nature of non-existence is itself the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This sutra further states that the Buddha said:
Kauśika! When good sons and good daughters proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā, there may be those who revile the Prajñāpāramitā.
What constitutes slandering the *prajñāpāramitā*? It is as follows:

to say that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure; and likewise to say that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), as well as the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), the noble truths (*āryasatya*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), and even up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure.
If one practices in such a manner, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To speak thus [of it otherwise] is to slander the perfection of wisdom.
What is it that does not slander the Prajñāpāramitā?
It is as follows: "O son of noble family! If one says:"

When you practice the perfection of wisdom, do not contemplate form as impermanent; do not contemplate form as suffering, selfless, or impure; and so it is for everything up to the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty.
If the intrinsic nature of form is empty, that is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If, within the *prajñāpāramitā*, form could be apprehended as permanent, then such form would not exist;
how much less could it be apprehended as either permanent or impermanent?
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One who speaks thus does not slander the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:
"O son of good family!
When you practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), do not think that there is any dharma to be transcended, nor think that there is any dharma in which to abide."
Why is this? Because within all phenomena (*dharma*), the *prajñāpāramitā* has no existence whatsoever.
If a phenomenon does not transcend non-abiding, then the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.
If the intrinsic nature of phenomena is empty, then phenomena are without intrinsic nature; if phenomena are without intrinsic nature, that is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Within this perfection of wisdom, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that emerges or enters, arises or ceases.
To speak in this manner is precisely not to slander the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, how can there be anything attained?
How can there be nothing attained?
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! If dharmas were dual, there would be something to be apprehended; if dharmas were non-dual, there would be nothing to be apprehended. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
What are these two?
The Buddha said:
Subhūti: "The eye and forms are two; the mind and mental phenomena are two; and so on, up to awakening and the Buddha-dharma, which are two. Subhūti said:
"Bhagavān! Is that which is 'something obtained' actually 'non-attainment'?
Or is it that which is 'non-attainment' that is truly 'non-attainment'?"
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, it is not that there is something to be attained which constitutes non-attainment, nor is it that there is nothing to be attained which constitutes non-attainment."
"Subhūti! Whether there is something attained or nothing attained, they are entirely equal; this is precisely what is meant by 'non-attainment.
Furthermore, Subhūti said:"
“World-Honored One!
Does one not abide within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) to realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said:
"No. Subhūti asked: "Do they abide within inverted dharmas?"
The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said:

If one does not abide in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), nor does one attain perfect enlightenment while abiding in inverted phenomena (*viparyāsa-dharma*), would it not follow that the Tathāgata has not realized the fruit of bodhi?
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! Although I have realized the fruit of bodhi, I abide nowhere within either the realm of the conditioned or the realm of the unconditioned."
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"Subhūti! I cannot attain perfect enlightenment by means of non-existence within non-existence."
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!
Is it not the case that within the nature of existence, the nature of non-existence can achieve perfect enlightenment?"
The Buddha said: "No. Subhūti said:
"If, within the absence of intrinsic nature, the absence of intrinsic nature itself could bring about perfect enlightenment, would that be possible? The Buddha said: "No."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I have previously said to you: "Subhūti!"
What do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?

Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any dharma that the Tathāgata can teach."
Why is this? If there were any dharma taught by the Tathāgata, it could not be grasped and could not be expressed; it would neither be a dharma nor a non-dharma. Why is that?
All worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

It is only for the sake of transforming and delivering sentient beings that the Tathāgata, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), opens various doors and proclaims such profound and correct Dharma.

As in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, when Mahāmati Bodhisattva questioned the Tathāgata regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, the Buddha said: "Mahāmati!"
Why do you now ask the Tathāgata about such teachings as "the intrinsic nature is luminous, pure, and primordially pure"?

The Tathāgata, endowed with the thirty-two marks, dwells within the bodies of all sentient beings; just as a priceless jewel might be wrapped and covered by coarse, filthy garments, so too is he enveloped by the garments of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.
Those unreal conceptual attachments of greed, hatred, and delusion—these defilements are impermanent phenomena, they are not solid, and they are not ultimate.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
Why can the discourse on the *ātman* (self) taught by the non-Buddhists not be equated with the discourse on the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Because the non-Buddhists assert that the *ātman* is eternal, capable of creative agency, independent and sovereign, and never subject to extinction.
They speak such words regarding a self (ātman).
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati!"
"Mahāmati, the Tīrthikas' discourse on 'self' (ātman) cannot be equated with the discourse on the *tathāgatagarbha*.

However, Mahāmati, when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak of such terms as the *bhūtakoṭi*, *nirvāṇa*, *anutpāda*, *śūnyatā*, *animitta*, and *apraṇihita*, they do so by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*) to teach the gate of the *tathāgatagarbha*— which is non-conceptual and free from all opposition— as a way to prevent ignorant beings from being terrified by the doctrine of selflessness."
In this regard, it is not that future or present bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are attached to what is produced by a self. Mahāmati!
It is like a potter who takes clay and turns it into mud; using water, a cord, and his tools, he exerts effort to produce various kinds of vessels.

The Tathāgata is likewise: dwelling in the selflessness of phenomena and free from the marks of conceptual discrimination, he employs various forms of superior wisdom and skillful means, sometimes teaching the *tathāgatagarbha* and sometimes teaching the dharma of selflessness, expounding through many exquisite, skillful phrases, expressions, and parables.
For this reason, the "discourse on self" (ātman-vāda) of the non-Buddhists cannot be equated with the discourse on the Tathāgatagarbha.

Mahāmati, furthermore, my discourse on the Tathāgatagarbha is taught solely as a skillful means to subdue those among the various non-Buddhists who cling to the discourse on a self; thus, I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha through such expedient means.
For what reason do such as these take pleasure in falling into views that falsely grasp at a non-existent self as a sovereign?
If one’s inclination is fully endowed with the three gates of liberation, one will be able to swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, the Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, cannot be compared to the discourse on the self (ātman) of the non-Buddhists.
Therefore, Mahāmati!

In order to cause the non-Buddhists to abandon their various views and attachments, so that they may attain the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s treasury of selflessness, that which is now proclaimed is called the supreme, perfected, and ultimate Dharma; it is called the Dharma of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and lack of intrinsic nature for all Bodhisattvas; it is called the profoundly deep Dharma.
If there are those who proclaim and uphold it, they will be able to universally encompass the profound meanings within all Mahāyāna sūtras. Why is this?
Because this profound Dharma is subsumed within all phenomena and all sūtras.
This sutra further states: "O Mahamati!
Because these characteristics of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and lack of intrinsic nature universally encompass all Buddhas and all sutras."
In the *Candrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra*, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:

"Within this trichiliocosm, all the various sūtras that I have proclaimed—though their phrases and expressions are manifold—they all possess a single meaning; therefore, it is impossible to explain them exhaustively."
Even all the Tathāgatas, and the many kinds of teachings they extensively proclaim—
having trained in them within a single phrase, one will achieve mastery in all practices.

All phenomena are of the nature of emptiness; if a person clearly understands this meaning, then through training in the significance of these words, the qualities of a Buddha will not be difficult to attain.
One who can have faith and understanding in the profound Dharma attains the arising of all supreme merit;
accomplishing all tasks, both mundane and supramundane, until the attainment of Buddhahood.

If each grain of sand in the river Gaṅgā were itself a river Gaṅgā, would the total number of grains of sand in all those rivers be great?
Subhūti said: "The Ganges Rivers themselves are already countless, how much more so their sands.

"By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit?
