"World-Honored One!
It is very much so. Sugata!"
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! If there is someone who, regarding this True Dharma, even receives and upholds a single four-line verse and explains it to others, their merit shall surpass that of the former."
The *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "O virtuous one!

If a son or daughter of good family delights in cultivating meritorious deeds in the presence of the Tathāgata, they should listen to, believe in, understand, and uphold this True Dharma; by doing so, they will obtain an abundance of physical beauty, numerous retinues, mastery over the Dharma, and experience all manner of happiness among gods and humans."
The *Śālistambha-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there should be a person who hears this exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā and, having heard it, develops faith and understanding, that person shall attain non-retrogression from Bodhi."
The Bodhisattva Maitreya said:
"World-Honored One!
If there are those who hear this exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā and, having heard it, believe and understand it, these bodhisattvas shall immediately attain proximity to the stage of Buddhahood."
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who hear this *prajñāpāramitā* being taught and, having heard it, believe and understand it, one should regard such bodhisattvas as being like the Buddha himself; all their sinful defilements and misdeeds will be completely resolved, all their karmic obstructions will become purified, and they will be able to give rise to supreme resolve regarding the profound Dharma.”
The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* states that the Buddha said: "Kāśyapa!
The most extreme among the ten unwholesome actions are as follows:"
First, if someone should commit the act of killing one whose father was a pratyekabuddha, this constitutes the most extreme offense of taking life.
Second, to plunder the property of the Triple Gem constitutes the most extreme offense of taking what is not given.
Third, if someone were to give rise to lustful attachment toward an Arhat as their mother, this would constitute the most extreme sin of sexual misconduct.
Fourth, if someone were to say, "I am the Tathāgata," and so forth, this would constitute the most extreme sin of lying.
Fifth, to create discord among the noble assembly is the most extreme offense of divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
Sixth, to revile the noble assembly is the most extreme offense of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
Seventh, to corrupt the desire for the true Dharma with worldly embellishments constitutes the most extreme offense of frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).

Eighth, to give rise to a mind of plundering toward the gains and offerings belonging to those who follow the right destination and the right path constitutes the most extreme offense of covetousness (*abhidhyā*).
Ninth, to praise the five deeds of immediate retribution is the most extreme sin of hatred.
Tenth, to give rise to perverse and evil views is the most extreme sin of wrong view.
Kāśyapa! These are the ten unwholesome karmas, all of which are extremely grave offenses. Kāśyapa!

If there is a single sentient being who possesses such transgressions and fully engages in the ten unwholesome actions, the Tathāgata will then proclaim for them the Dharma of the harmony of causes and conditions, causing them to understand and enter it; at that time, they will likewise be free from the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

If one can understand that these phenomena are unconditioned, uncreated, and like an illusion—stainless, pure, and luminous by nature—and understands that all phenomena are primordially pure, then for those sentient beings who possess pure faith and resolute conviction in all phenomena, I do not say they will fall into the evil realms.
Why is this? Because no inherent nature of an aggregate of afflictions can be found; as soon as they arise, they are immediately shattered and dispersed.
Therefore, one should know that all afflictions are produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions, and having arisen, they perish instantly.
If one gives rise to the thought of dispelling them, the afflictions will immediately arise again.
If one has such faith and understanding, what further [affliction] could there be?
For there is no place where the state of sin can find accommodation.
If one were to say that it is possible for those with various karmic obstacles to dwell [in this state], such a thing is impossible.
As the Venerable Upāli, the Master of the Vinaya, asked in the "Chapter on Subduing Māra": "O you evil Māras!"
"What is it that constitutes a bhikṣu who truly upholds the practice of the Vinaya?
Māra said: "Venerable One!"
If a bhikṣu thoroughly understands that all phenomena are ultimately tamed, and that all transgressions are fundamentally without beginning or end because they are free from limits;
then, even if he commits a *pāyattika* offense or other *duṣkṛta* offenses, he should completely release them and not give rise to stubborn attachment.
If one reveals such a Dharma to others, even their five sins of immediate retribution will be entirely eliminated, let alone minor transgressions or the defilements of broken precepts.

One who understands these laws and regulations is not defiled by adventitious afflictions and gives rise to the thought of renunciation; they know that all afflictions are neither internal, nor external, nor in between. It is not that the wisdom free from defilement can eliminate afflictions, for the nature of being free from defilement is itself not something to be discarded.
The wise observe all afflictions as they truly are: like clouds driven by the wind, dispersing and scattering, toward whichever direction they may go, where could they ever settle?
Furthermore, all afflictions are like the moon in water; they appear before one as the reflections of pervasive conceptualization.
Furthermore, all afflictions are realms of darkness, which the radiant light of the lamp of wisdom can illuminate and shatter.

Moreover, the thieves of the afflictions stealthily harm physical forms like yakṣas and rākṣasas; yet, if one applies firm and stable attention to observe them as they truly are, they will find no place to abide.

Furthermore, the various afflictions are constantly watching for an opportunity; if one does not maintain firm and stable mental attention (*manasikāra*), the afflictions will increase, whereas within the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), they cannot cause harm or opposition.

Furthermore, regarding these very afflictions, a wise person, through their wisdom, stands before those sentient beings who are attached to such afflictions and, giving rise to a heart of compassion, teaches them the Dharma of non-self and the absence of sentient beings to cause them to abandon defilement; this is what constitutes the true upholding of the Vinaya.
The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* states that the Buddha said: "Ānanda!

I now tell you this in truth: if there should be one who has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), yet upon hearing such a sublime Dharma is able to give rise to resolute faith (*adhimukti*), I do not say that such a person possesses karma or karmic obstructions."

Ānanda! To speak in brief, regarding this profound and sublime Dharma that has been proclaimed, you should give rise to resolute faith, offer vast praise, and listen to it with diligent application in various sūtras again and again.

A bodhisattva who does not depart from skillful means should thus diligently practice the teaching of the profound Dharma; therefore, wisdom and skillful means are inseparable, and this constitutes the bodhisattva’s correspondence with the True Dharma.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation.
What is meant by "wisdom without skillful means is bondage"?

If a bodhisattva disciplines the mind within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet does not adorn buddha-fields with the marks and signs of excellence nor bring sentient beings to maturity, this is precisely what is called "wisdom without skillful means is bondage."
What is meant by liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means?

If a bodhisattva can adorn buddha-fields with the primary and secondary marks and bring sentient beings to maturity, while taming their minds within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, practicing with diligence and vigor without weariness—this is what is called liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
What is called the bondage of skillful means lacking wisdom?

If a bodhisattva gives rise to and pursues various views and afflictions, dwelling with attachment to them, yet nevertheless initiates all roots of goodness and dedicates them toward unsurpassed enlightenment—this is precisely what is meant by the bondage of skillful means lacking wisdom.
What is meant by "liberation through wisdom and skillful means"?

If a bodhisattva, while arising from and following after various views and afflictions, severs all attachments to existence, and gives rise to all roots of goodness, dedicating them toward unsurpassed enlightenment without grasping at anything whatsoever—this is what is called liberation through wisdom and skillful means.
One should know that the union of these two dharmas—wisdom and skillful means—is entirely the practice of a bodhisattva.
What is the practice of a bodhisattva?
It is that which is neither the practice of ordinary worldlings nor the practice of noble sages; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To remain within birth and death without being defiled, and to remain within nirvana without entering eternal quiescence—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Though seeking the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, not to realize nirvana prematurely—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To contemplate internal emptiness while constantly intending to manifest birth within the three realms of existence is the bodhisattva practice.
To contemplate non-arising without entering the stage of certainty is the bodhisattva practice.
To gather all sentient beings without being stained by attachment is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice within emptiness while constantly and diligently seeking the merits of all marks is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice non-action while diligently cultivating all wholesome deeds and attaining pliancy is the bodhisattva practice.
To cultivate the practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā without ultimately falling into cessation is the bodhisattva practice.
Although they turn the wheel of Dharma and manifest great parinirvāṇa, they do not abandon the practices performed by bodhisattvas; this is the bodhisattva practice.
All such instances as these are the practices performed by bodhisattvas.
The *Māradamanasūtra* states:

Furthermore, all that constitutes the supreme correct practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas is as follows: namely, the superior application of transcendent wisdom (*prajñā*), and the skillful means (*upāya*) wisdom which universally encompasses the practice of all wholesome dharmas.

The wisdom of supreme insight is the absence of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-force, a soul, and so forth; the wisdom of skillful means is the practice of bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
The wisdom of supreme insight (*prajñā*) is the practice that universally encompasses all phenomena; the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*) is the practice of correctly embracing the True Dharma.

The wisdom of supreme insight is the non-conceptual practice regarding the entire realm of all Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom of skillful means is the practice of honoring, making offerings to, and serving all Buddha-dharmas.

The one with supreme wisdom and knowledge practices the conduct of all buddha-fields as being like space; the one with skillful means and knowledge practices the conduct of purifying the ornaments of merit in all buddha-fields.

The wisdom of superior intelligence is the practice of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) cultivated by all noble ones (ārya); the wisdom of skillful means is the practice of generating a mind of reverence toward all teachers and honoring them through various forms of service.
The one with supreme wisdom observes the untainted conduct of the Buddha’s body; the one with skillful means cultivates the conduct of the Buddha’s marks and signs.

The one with supreme wisdom observes the conduct of all phenomena being unborn and unarisen; the one with skillful means constantly contemplates the conduct of manifesting birth within the three realms of existence.
The *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "What is the skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva?
And what is their superior wisdom (*prajñā*)? It is as follows:
when entering meditative absorption, one gives rise to a profound and firm mind that takes great compassion as its object and observes sentient beings; this is skillful means."
If, while abiding in meditative concentration, one dwells in stillness and universal tranquility, this is transcendent wisdom (*prajñā*).
If, upon entering concentration, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in accordance with the Buddha-way, this is skillful means (*upāya*).
If one relies on and observes that which is non-existent, this is transcendent wisdom.
If, when entering meditative concentration, one observes the universal inclusion of all those phenomena, this is skillful means;
if one observes the dharma-realm as being without differentiation, this is transcendent wisdom.
When, upon entering meditative absorption, the manifestations of the Buddha’s bodily adornments appear before one, this is skillful means;
when one observes the stages of the Dharma-body, this is superior wisdom.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states that the Buddha said:

"Maitreya! A bodhisattva has two characteristics: first, delighting in various phrases and literary embellishments; second, not fearing the most profound dharmas and entering into them through correct understanding. These are the two characteristics."
If a bodhisattva places their faith, delight, and respect in miscellaneous phrases and ornate literary embellishments, one should know that this is a beginner bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if they listen to, receive, proclaim, and develop resolute conviction in these pure and profound sūtras—which universally encompass the various gateways of diverse words and meanings—one should know that this bodhisattva has long practiced the holy life.
Furthermore, there are two things that cause a beginner bodhisattva to bring harm upon themselves and fail to discipline their mind within the profound Dharma.
First, regarding profound sūtras never heard before, upon hearing them, they become terrified and give rise to doubt, failing to accord with them; instead, they produce disparaging slander, saying:
"I have never heard this before; from where has this Dharma come?"

Second, they do not delight in associating with, nor do they respect, those sons of good family who proclaim the profound Dharma to those who are great vessels for it; at times, they even secretly speak of their faults.
These are the two dharmas.

Furthermore, there are two other dharmas by which a bodhisattva, despite having faith and understanding in the extremely profound Dharma, nonetheless brings himself harm and is unable to swiftly realize the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
First, they disparage beginner bodhisattvas, failing to embrace them, failing to provide definitive analysis for them, and failing to instruct them.

Second, although they have faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, they do not study it nor do they honor it; furthermore, they do not practice the giving of material wealth or the giving of the Dharma to embrace sentient beings.
These are the two dharmas.
In this regard, it should be understood that for sentient beings to understand and enter into the great majestic power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is extremely difficult to attain.
What constitutes the great majestic power of a bodhisattva?
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that Vimalakīrti said: "Mahākāśyapa!"

All those who currently manifest as Māras throughout the worlds of the ten directions are bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation; they manifest the form of a Māra for the sake of maturing sentient beings through skillful means.

Furthermore, in the worlds of the ten directions, there may be bodhisattvas from whom others beg for their hands, feet, ears, noses, blood, flesh, tendons, bones, heads, eyes, limbs, wives, children, slaves, servants, subjects, cities, and nations, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages.
To all such seekers who come to him, he gives and bestows everything.
Because he acts with such a manner of compulsion, these are all bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation.
Kāśyapa! It is like this:
for example, when a dragon-elephant tramples, it is not something a donkey can endure.
Ordinary persons are just like this; they cannot thus oppress a bodhisattva, whereas a bodhisattva is indeed able to thus oppress a bodhisattva.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the section on the stages of the Dharma-realm practices and vows, it is proclaimed that the Bodhisattva Infinite Buddha-Seed World Honored One, the Tathāgata Universal Wisdom Realm Sound, came from that land before the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Tathāgata, manifesting the majestic physical form of a bodhisattva—namely, complete with all limbs, all marks and signs, all pores, all adornments, all vestments and requisites, and the full assembly of all bodhisattva retinues.

All the Blessed Ones—the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana abiding in the past limit, all the Tathāgatas of the past abiding in the future limit, all the Tathāgatas of the future who have received or have not yet received their predictions, and all the Bodhisattvas universally dwelling in all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions of the present—all these manifest as reflections within the ocean of prior practices associated with the perfection of giving that they cultivated in the past. All recipients and all objects given are fully reflected therein; likewise, all bodily forms, all pores, and all the marks and signs are also clearly manifested and displayed.
Furthermore, all bodily postures, modes of speech, and the array of clothing, ornaments, and various requisites are also manifested and displayed individually. Moreover,
there is the ocean of past practices associated with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*),
as well as the ocean of past practices associated with the manifestation of bodily mutilations through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), and furthermore...
The ocean of prior practices associated with the diligence of a bodhisattva’s application;
furthermore, the ocean of prior practices associated with the vast meditative concentrations and the accomplishment of activities of all Tathāgatas;

and furthermore, the ocean of prior practices associated with each representation of the manifested gateways of the sovereign bodily forms that relinquish all possessions, which accomplish the dharma-activities of all Tathāgatas turning the great wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the ocean of the preliminary practices associated with the supreme love and joy of all worlds, through which all Tathāgatas joyfully behold the bodhisattva path;
furthermore, there is the ocean of the preliminary practices associated with the vast adornments of the superior dharma-gates that increase the ocean of the various sublime vows of all bodhisattvas;
furthermore, there is the accomplishment of the various practices of the bodhisattvas’ perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

The ocean of preliminary practices corresponding to pure accomplishment, as well as the vehicle of the ocean of preliminary practices corresponding to the cognitive domain of the bodhisattvas’ vast activities—
the clouds of all miraculous transformations throughout the great dharma-realm of the bodhisattvas—
these represent the manifestation of the ten *pāramitās*.

Clouds of all manner of vast and magnificent spiritual transformations from throughout the entire great dharma-realm came to the place where the Buddha was. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, together with his retinue, prostrated before the Buddha and stationed themselves above him. Within a great celestial palace named the Treasury of Adornments of the Heart of All Vajra-Indra Jewels—which he had miraculously manifested—he sat cross-legged upon a lion throne of Vajra-Indra-blue lotuses. He appeared covered by a net of various jewel-flame *maṇi* kings, further adorned by hanging necklaces of the King of Jewels of the Voices of all Tathāgatas of the three times. Wearing a *maṇi* jewel crown upon his head, he remained there, manifesting the body of a Bodhisattva through empowerment.

This Bodhisattva, together with his retinue, is born from the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; he manifests purity within the gateway of the feet of all Tathāgatas, and through the eye of wisdom, he perceives and hears the ocean of sublime sounds of the principles and teachings within the Dharma wheels of all Tathāgatas. He universally gathers all Bodhisattvas who have attained various masteries and have achieved the supreme *pāramitās*.
All Tathāgatas gathered like clouds, manifesting vast miraculous transformations in every single moment, and appearing within the expansive realms of the bodies of all sentient beings.

The light from the bodies within the assemblies and *bodhimaṇḍas* of all Tathāgatas illuminates all worlds; within a single world, it universally reflects and manifests all objective phenomena like a mass of motes of dust. All sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured and who are ready for deliverance through transformation are able to appear in response at the appropriate time.

The clouds of the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Tathāgatas, the realm of the roaring sounds from all pores, pervading all worlds and giving rise to all roots of goodness—once arisen, they instantly become equal throughout the bodies of all sentient beings, and within a single moment of focused mind, they extensively manifest miraculous transformations as oceans of clouds across all directions.

This sutra further states: Regarding the Bodhisattva’s power of great majestic virtue, at that time the youth Sudhana gazed intently upon the physical marks and features of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. He then clearly perceived each and every constituent part of the Bodhisattva’s body; each and every constituent part was distinct. Each and every realm-body was clearly distinguished in its subtle divisions; each and every bodily member was clearly distinguished in its respective positions. Each and every collection of supports was clearly distinguished; each and every pore was clearly distinguished.

He manifested all the elements of wind, fire, and earth within this trichiliocosm, including the great oceans, islands, rivers, and jeweled mountains, as well as Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), and so forth; the lands, cities, villages, regions, forests, and dwellings; the various populations; and the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; the realms of the asuras, nāgas, garuḍas, humans, devas, and the Brahma realm; and the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
All these realms abide through the empowerment of spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This extends to forms and colors, clouds, lightning, and the stars; to day and night, the full moon, the crescent moon, seasons, and years; and to the kalpas of abiding and the kalpas of destruction.

Having manifested such characteristics of this world-system, one likewise observes all world-systems in the eastern direction; and in the same manner, all world-systems in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below appear before one as they are observed.

Furthermore, within every single body of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, one sees all the marks of greatness, as well as the birthplaces of all Buddhas, the assemblies and sites of enlightenment, and all the dwellings of sentient beings throughout this Sahā world; one also sees the entirety of the past, from the beginningless limit through the present, including all the mutual interactions of all worlds, as well as the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Bodhisattvas at the time of the Buddhas' births, and the houses of sentient beings, along with their days, nights, and kalpas.

In this same way, throughout the future limit, all Buddha-fields and world-systems everywhere are likewise; in all of them, one sees the reflections of all worlds—past, future, and present—mutually appearing within one another, just as they do here in this Sahā world.

In this way, throughout all worlds existing in the past, future, and present across the ten directions, they all saw within each and every body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva the marks of a great man; within each and every pore, these were clearly distinct and mutually unmixed. They all saw Samantabhadra Bodhisattva before the World-Honored One, Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, seated upon a lion throne within a great jewel lotus treasury, manifesting playful spiritual powers.
At that time, the Tathāgata Bhadraśrī in the world Padmaśrī to the east beheld this manifested play of supernatural powers.

As it was in the east, so it was throughout all worlds in the ten directions; in each case, they all saw the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra seated upon a great precious lotus-treasury lion throne within the foot-root gates of every Tathāgata, manifesting these playful supernatural powers.

Just as in all worlds throughout the ten directions, one sees within the foot-roots of all Tathāgatas the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra seated upon a great lion throne within a precious lotus-flower treasury, manifesting these playful supernatural powers.

At that time, throughout all Buddha-fields in the ten directions as numerous as atoms, each of which was a site of enlightenment for a vast Dharma-realm assembly of Buddhas as numerous as those very atoms, he saw in the foot-roots of every Tathāgata the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra seated upon a great lion throne within a precious lotus-womb treasury, manifesting these playful supernatural powers.

At that time, every single bodily form fully attained the manifestation of the reflected images of all objects of perception throughout the three times; it manifested as the reflections of all buddha-fields, all sentient beings, the descents of all Buddhas, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas at their sites of enlightenment.

At that time, one hears the speech of all sentient beings, the voices of all Buddhas, the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma by all Tathāgatas, the proclamation of all instructions and the sounds of all supernatural transformations, and the sounds of the assemblies of all Bodhisattvas and the spheres of the playful manifestations of all Buddhas—in brief, as it has been described, one should know that all these are the power of the great majestic virtue of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
In this regard, one should ask:
What is the Tathāgata’s power of great majestic virtue?
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
O Son of the Buddha!
Since the realms of the bodhisattvas' practices are thus, and their sustaining spiritual powers are still immeasurable, how can they enter the realm of the Tathāgata’s practice?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha,
it is as if someone were to take two or three small pebbles, the size of beans, from among the worlds of the four great continents, and speak thus:"
Is there perhaps any world-system greater than this,
or is it immeasurable?
To speak such words is like comparing the dharmas of the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas with the dharmas of Bodhisattvas at this present time.
O Son of the Buddha!
The four great continents of this world are like a tiny fragment of a stone the size of a *māṣa* bean that has been picked up; the remainder is immeasurable.
The realm of the Tathāgata is likewise so.

Furthermore, even if one were to spend immeasurable eons, one could not describe even a small fraction of the merits possessed by a Bodhisattva on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā), let alone the realm of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha, I now speak these true words to you; may the Tathāgata bear witness for me.

Suppose that all the Buddha-fields in the infinite worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, were filled with those who have realized the stages of a Bodhisattva, as dense as groves of rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, and sugarcane.

Even if those bodhisattvas were to spend boundless eons expounding and elucidating all the spheres of knowledge of the Tathāgata, they would not equal even one hundredth part of it; nor would they equal even one part in ten million, nayuta, hundred-thousand, or any part expressible by analogy.
The *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!
Within this assembly, there may be sentient beings who say that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, first went forth into homelessness; or..."
Some have long since left the household life; some are said to be practicing various ascetic penances; some are seated at the site of enlightenment having attained equal and perfect awakening;
some have defeated the armies of Māra; some are being exhorted by Brahmā, Śakra, and the world-protectors to turn the great wheel of Dharma;
some hear the proclamation of the vehicle of the śrāvakas; some hear the teaching of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; or some hear...

In the Mahāyāna Dharma, some behold the Buddha’s body at a height of one *vyāma*, some see the Buddha’s body at a height of one *krośa*, and some see the Buddha’s body manifesting at a height exceeding hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.
Some see the Buddha’s body as the color of pure gold, and even some see it as the color of a *maṇi* jewel; or they may see it...
They may see the Tathāgata’s tranquil physical form; or they may see the Tathāgata entering the state of parinirvāṇa;
or they may see the Tathāgata as a single unified body; or they may see the distribution of the Tathāgata’s relics.
Some may say that he attained perfect enlightenment ten years ago, or that he entered great parinirvāṇa ten years ago, or that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni still exists in the world.
Among those who have attained perfection within the teachings of the Muni Tathāgata,
some have passed away, while others are said to enter great parinirvāṇa after ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or even hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas;
or it is said that the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, attained [Buddhahood] after unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas.
“Samyaksaṃbuddha! Mañjuśrī,
regarding such various differentiated characteristics, the Tathāgata neither discriminates nor is free from discrimination.”

Yet the Buddha-Tathāgata, by means of the dharma that is without arousal of thought and without discrimination, constantly manifests various modes of activity in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
"O Mañjuśrī!..."

There are various explanations; for instance, there is a great pond, fifty thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, its shores level and its waters clear and sweet, with lotus flowers covering its entire surface.

Suppose there were someone who, having fashioned an iron chariot with a thousand spokes, yoked it to swift horses possessing a speed more rapid than that of a garuḍa; as that chariot travels, it does not touch the waters of the ponds, nor do the horses' hooves tread upon the lotuses.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this.

He rides upon a great chariot and travels across that great pond. Within it, there is a venomous snake that stirs the water and leaps up; if, in a single kṣaṇa, that venomous snake turns to follow behind the chariot, the chariot immediately circles to the right seven times.
Furthermore, if a venomous snake were to circle a great chariot once to the right, that chariot would immediately circle countless times to the right.

It is the same with the preaching of the Dharma by great bhikṣus such as Ānanda: sometimes Ānanda expresses the meaning by teaching ten kinds of dharmas, yet if Ānanda teaches even a single dharma, Śāriputra immediately expresses its meaning by teaching a thousand kinds of dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, while he speaks a single dharma, Mahāmaudgalyāyana instantly traverses eighty thousand worlds.
Furthermore, while Mahāmaudgalyāyana traverses a single world, the Tathāgata—
supremely sovereign over the dharma-realms of the ten directions and transcending the limits of space— pervades all oceans of worlds, in each and every world...
In every realm, on every island-continent, and within every path of ordinary beings, he manifests the descent from the Tuṣita heaven, his entry into the human world,
his entry into the womb, his dwelling in the womb, and his birth from the womb; he is received, bathed,
and adorned by Brahmā kings and Śakra devendra, takes seven steps in every direction, surveys the ten quarters, and utters the lion’s roar.

He studied all crafts, arts, sciences, and worldly activities; he manifested the status of a crown prince, sporting and enjoying himself within the royal palace and strolling through gardens; he left the home life and practiced austerities;
having consumed the milk-rice gruel, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment and sat there to achieve perfect awakening; he subdued the armies of Māra and gazed at the tree.
In his conduct, he was invited by the Great Brahma Heaven King to turn the Wheel of Dharma and entered the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and so forth.

Regarding the dimensions of his lands, the sequence of eons, his majestic virtue, physical marks, and the extent of his lifespan; the adornments of his assemblies and the purity of his Buddha-fields; the adornment of his teachings and the inspiring of the bodhicitta; the cultivation of various practices and vows to fulfill the pāramitās; the perfection of all stages, supernatural powers, wisdom, and patience; and his possession of dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and all doors of liberation.

The Tathāgatas are immeasurable; the various acts of making offerings are immeasurable; the dharma-sphere of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas is immeasurable; the extent of their practice within the vast clouds of Dharma is immeasurable; the distinctions in the stages of skillful means for maturing sentient beings are immeasurable; they give rise to great playful displays of supernatural powers and transformations, manifesting the Great Parinirvāṇa of the One Vehicle, and distributing relics while differentiating the teachings.
The duration of his stay, as well as the time when the Dharma shall perish, all emerge from this great pool of the sublime Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the places where non-Buddhists practice their disciplines and all the tasks that sentient beings ought to perform, the Tathāgata—by means of a mind free from conceptualization and without deliberate effort—manifests them all simultaneously, displaying diligent exertion throughout the final limit of existence.

In every such instant, simultaneously within each and every pore of his own body throughout the ten directions, there appeared the oceans of assemblies of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas pervading all spatial quarters and the three periods of time; the vast arrays of merit and adornments of all Buddha-fields; the vast arrays of dwellings, palaces, and residences of the multitudes of sentient beings; the vast establishments of the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind of the multitudes of sentient beings; the vast arrays accumulated through all the practices of Bodhisattvas; and the vast arrays of the spheres of all Tathāgatas.
Such signs as these, the Tathāgata simultaneously and universally manifests with a mind that is both non-aroused and non-discriminative.

At the final limit, in a single moment of ultimate diligence, he universally encompasses all worlds of the ten directions, including even the paths of ordinary beings—whether finite or infinite—without leaving anything remaining.

Regarding all sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings, for each and every being, the Tathāgata simultaneously and universally manifests—by means of a mind that is without arousal and free from discrimination—all such distinctions of measure as their individual bodily forms, shapes, colors, voices, languages, parables, and methods of teaching the Dharma.

In accordance with the various and distinct mentalities of sentient beings, one should apply oneself with ultimate diligence until the very end, manifesting and acting in whatever way is appropriate. Mañjuśrī!

For example, at midnight on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, throughout Jambudvīpa, all men, women, boys, and girls each perceive the form of the lunar disc before them, yet that lunar disc remains entirely without discrimination.

The Tathāgata is likewise: with a mind free from arousal and free from discrimination, he manifests the signs of all activities. Because he has accomplished the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), he transforms and delivers sentient beings according to their mental dispositions and as is appropriate. While every sentient being perceives the Tathāgata appearing before them individually, the Tathāgata’s mind remains without discrimination.

Therefore, you should know that whether there is conceptualization or non-conceptualization, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are entirely without [deliberate] awakening; yet, because they have accomplished the unshared Buddha-dharmas, they perform all modes of activity as appropriate to the occasion.
In this regard, it should be understood that within the vast and profound sūtras, the great majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is uniquely and explicitly revealed.
If there are those who can develop deep faith and understanding, and who copy, read, recite, honor, and make offerings to them, such persons will obtain vast and immeasurable merit.
This sutra further states: The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!

For example, it is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which rises above all other mountains; its brilliant illumination is exquisite, and it is both high and vast, being moreover the greatest of all."
Mañjuśrī! It is likewise for a bodhisattva who has faith and understanding in this true Dharma; such a one surpasses all other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Suppose there were as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and they were to develop faith and understanding in this true Dharma. All the roots of goodness produced by their five pāramitās, accumulated over asaṃkhyeya kalpas—though they be brilliant, exquisite, lofty, vast, and supreme—[would still not equal the merit of this].

Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were to exhort all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions to resolve upon bodhicitta, and if there were another son or daughter of good family who, with faith and joy, aspires toward nirvāṇa without remainder, the merit obtained by the latter would be many times greater than that of the former, beyond measure.

Mañjuśrī! Suppose a son or daughter of good family were to cause all sentient beings, without exception, to have faith and joy in *nirvāṇa* without remainder; yet, if another son or daughter of good family were able to give rise to faith and joy in this True Dharma—whether by writing it themselves or causing others to write it, whether by reading and reciting it themselves or causing others to read and recite it, or even merely being able to believe, rejoice in, and uphold it—and were to make offerings to it with various requisites such as incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments, the merit obtained from this would be many times greater than the former, beyond all calculation.
